speechtext:
I should like to speak on a question of privilege affecting this parliament and a committee of parliament. It has to do with a letter which is being sent through the mails bearing. the signature of Tom L. Poulsom, Rochfort Bridge, Alberta. From time to time since the session started members of parliament have drawn to my attention copies of this letter which they have received by mail from constituents. They have suggested that as the conduct of the special select committee on veterans affairs for 1946 is called in question, as chairman of that committee I should make a statement. I had hoped that the sending out of these letters would cease and perhaps a statement would not need to be made. However these letters seem to be still going out so I decided I should give the facts to the house.
This letter makes general accusations of forgery and theft against the soldier settlement board. It suggests that the veterans affairs committee should have called him, Poulsom, as a witness, and that in not doing so, criminal civil servants, in his words, were being "shielded" and "wet-nursed" and that swindling of the veteran, dominion treasury and taxpayer was being permitted to go unchecked by members of parliament.
At the start of its work the veterans affairs committee, in accordance with the usual practice, set up a steering committee. This committee, consisting of Messrs. Green, Brooks, Wright, Quelch, Croll, Tremblay and myself, was to decide, among other things, on what witnesses should be called. When Poulsom made his first accusation, pursuant to instructions by the steering committee I asked him to send details of his charges giving specific facts, names, dates, places and details; otherwise the committee would not consider them. Mr. Poulsom's response was to repeat his general charges.
The steering committee thereupon on May 23, 1946, further considered the matter. It had formerly decided that so much work lay before it that it was doubtful if it could be completed no matter how assiduously the committee worked. The steering committee had there-

fore recommended to the committee as a whole that no individual case would be heard unless same was sponsored by some representative organization. This recommendation had been communicated to the committee as a whole and was accepted and approved by the committee. The committee, as the house knows, consisted of sixty members of parliament, all ex-servicemen. In view of this policy of the committee and the further fact that Poulsom had not been willing to bring forward a single fact to substantiate his general charges or even to make a. specific charge of wrong-doing, the steering committee on May 23, 1946, decided to recommend that Mr. Poulsom be informed of the committee's policy not to hear representations from individuals unless sponsored by representative veteran organizations or other responsible bodies. This recommendation of the steering committee was concurred in on May 23, 1946, by the committee itself on a motion duly made and carried. References to the matter may be found in the records of our proceedings of May 21 and 23.
From the foregoing, it will be seen that my actions in the matter were taken on the instructions of the committee itself.
To the extent that Mr. Poulsom's charges relate to his own dealings with, the soldier settlement board the director reports as follows: T. L. Poulsom was established under the Soldier Settlement Act by an agreement for sale dated October 16, 1919. Due to his failure to live up to his agreement he was served with notice of rescission of contract on December 8, 1942. Poulsom's appeal was heard by Judge Matheson at Edmonton on March 29, 1943. Matters in dispute were fully heard. Poulsom's solicitor was J. Boyd McBride, K.C. A final settlement was reached between Poulsom and the board.
Confirmation of the settlement is contained in an official letter dated March 29, 1943, from Poulsom's solicitor to the district superintendent at Edmonton in part as follows:
This is a final and absolute settlement of all points which heretofore have been in dispute extending over a period of many years . . . this letter has been dictated in Mr. Poulsom's presence.
The director reports that he has carried out his part of these proposals.
He also reports that Mr. Poulsom has from time to time circulated charges against the soldier settlement administration alleging perjury, forgery, theft and other crimes. The director reports that there is no evidence in departmental records indicating that any of the alleged offences have been committed by members of the departmental staff, but if Mr. MAY 6, 1947
Privilege-Mr. Stuart
Poulsom thinks any offence has been committed, he may lay a charge before a magistrate. He was invited to do so a year previously, but no such action has been taken by him.
So far as I am concerned I repudiate any suggestion that our veterans affairs committee shielded any wrongdoer. Such a suggestion is most unfair and unjust to the members of this house who were members of our veterans affairs committee. Poulsom was given a chance to make a specific charge. He refused to do so but continues to circulate his general charges. These charges are of such a general nature that it would be difficult for anyone to take action on them to disprove them, and so they are unfair to the civil servants involved. They are also unfair to a committee of ex-servicemen who did a great deal of work in two sessions considering and recommending legislation to improve the programme for the rehabilitation and reestablishment of our exservicemen and women. I need hardly say that in the course of its work our committee protected or shielded nobody.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, April 29, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall have to ask some indulgence from the house today because I have been ill and have not been able to prepare myself as I would have liked. However, the house will at least benefit, inasmuch as I shall not speak as long as I otherwise would.
When we adjourned on Tuesday last we were in what I suppose might be called a sort of sunshine atmosphere. The budget which the minister had read was one which it so happened that most of us in this chamber were able to benefit from, and we were inclined to think well of it. But I am inclined to think that as time has gone on there are people who began to reflect and as other considerations entered into the matter some misgivings may have entered their minds and they may not be quite so sure that all is well.
I do not intend to labour again the question of the surplus. That has been dealt with, and I have no doubt will be dealt with again. I think really it was a bit of good clean fun, but it does occur to me that if some of the finance ministers of former days, men like Mr. Fielding and Sir George Foster, were able to come and ask the minister, "Is it really true that you were able to have a surplus which was

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
made up by selling things which you had not had to pay for out of taxes, which were paid for out of borrowed money?" and if the minister had said, as he would have said, "Yes, that is quite true," they would have said, "Well, these are rather strange and wonderful days; you have certainly progressed beyond the days when we lived."
What should we ask of a budget? What is it for? Obviously, first of all, it is a statement of the country's expected receipts and disbursements, and also it is a statement of any changes in taxation. In the second place, and perhaps just as important, it should try to give us, and the minister did at considerable length, a picture of the country's position -not merely a set of figures, although they are important, but an attempt to try to make the people of the country understand the situation that they are facing. In the old days when one year merged into another, and there was practically no change except a few dollars here or there, that was not of great importance, but in a year like this, when we stand on the verge of so many new and strange things, it becomes of vast importance. Later on I shall have some things to say about that.
I come now to the matter of the budget, and I want to say one or two things about it. We have a measure of taxation relief which has been given to a group of people in the country that I think deserve great consideration, people whom I call-I am speaking now of people with incomes of from $3,000 to $7,500-the middle class. It seems to me that all history shows that where the middle class is strong, then the state is strong. Where the middle class disintegrates and disappears, then the state is weak. I want to come back to that.
At the moment all I say is that I welcome- I hope it is not an entirely selfish remark when I make it-what the minister did. My only regret is that there were other things that were not done. My only regret is. and I shall have more to say about this later, that it seems that the minister has taken the view that he cannot do anything for business because business is doing pretty well and therefore he would just let well enough alone, until the end of the year at any rate. There is another great class in the community which is affected mainly by indirect taxes such as sales and others for which nothing has been done. Indeed their position at the present moment is being rather worsened.
I know the difficulties that have arisen, and I sympathize with the minister because of his position at the present time. This is perhaps a difficult moment for advantages to
be given to others and not to these people because at the present time they are suffering from nothing more than this: I fear that during the war they got the idea that there was never going to be any readjustment, that the big money was going to go on, that somehow or other they could have big money and that prices would be kept down. In other words, they thought they were going to have it both ways.
At the moment it is particularly unfortunate that we here who believe in removing controls, and I am one of those, at the present time are at a most unsatisfactory moment, as you might say, from the point of view of the people of the class of which I am speaking. We are in a period when there is bound to be a certain shaking out of prices, a certain inequality. In the United States they are beginning to get the benefit of production and I am glad to observe that for the last three weeks the trend of prices has definitely been downward. We have not that condition here as we would like to have it, and therefore at the moment we have the unfortunate situation, to which I shall refer again, that the minister has done absolutely nothing- I think that is a fair statement-to take measures to meet the difficulties which notwithstanding his optimistic statement he himself sees only too clearly.
Having said that, I wish to say also that while the minister has put in many caveats- I am going to read one or two of them- while the minister has brought out this and that difficulty, nevertheless as a whole the minister's line is that things are good, that things are booming, that everything is going well and that all we need to do is to keep along in that way. I want to point out first of all that the minister is cautious. He has several caveats here and I shall read one or two of them. He said:
... We must also recognize the special and temporary character of much of the expenditure that is the stimulus of our present high level of income . . .
He says again:
Much of the large expenditure of business on plant and equipment represents accumulated or postponed requirements and does not give us any reliable guidance as to what we may expect on a continuing basis.
Again he says:
Consumers, too, are probably . . . spending more and saving less than they normally would with incomes at present levels.
All these things he says, and yet I leave it to anyone who heard or read his speech that the general tenor left in our minds was that we are virtually in the midst of a boom; that
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell

we ought to be satisfied and extremely happy, that there is nobody on the whole who should be more contented than we are, and of course that is correct. Nevertheless I am not satisfied with the position which the minister gave.
If you will remember, the minister talked constantly about money, money. He measured things in terms of money; he measured progress in terms of money. I have had for many years a friend whose business it was to try to gauge the course of business in various countries of the world, and he always used to say to me, "Don't talk to me money. Talk to me commodities. Talk to me quantities of goods-real things." Therefore when I find the minister saying as he did say and' apparently confining himself to that, that our national income was such and such, I say: Don't talk to me national income. I say talk to me commodities, goods, quantities of this and that.
The minister laid great stress on the fact that our income had gone up from 1939, when it was $5-5 billion, to 1947, when it was $11-1 billion. That sounds in a way quite magnificent. You will say we have doubled our national income. And not a word was said to warn us:	Oh, but there is a great catch in
this. You must remember that the money is twice as big but the quantities are not twice as much, the goods are not. twice as much. Though I confess it is hard to arrive at the true correcting figure, nevertheless if you take the rise in prices and apply them you will reduce that S11T billion of money to something not very far from S7-5 billion in goods. If that is correct then the increase from 1939 is not double, from $5-5 to $11T; it is really from $5-5 to something like $7-5 billion. What does that mean? That to me is the explanation of what we hear every day, of what we have dinned into our ears every day. It is the explanation of shortages and I confess I have found it perplexing. That is why we hear everywhere and every day that something or other is short, and we all do hear it. Therefore I suggest that when we talk about this figure of money, when we deal only with that and talk only of national income, we are dealing with something which is illusory, something which means nothing until you begin to define it.
And so I say that this situation which the minister shows us is not anything like as good as those figures would indicate. In fact it is a very dangerous situation because it is a situation such as was described to the British people in a white paper that said something like 'this. They said that in England there are seven billion pounds of money chasing around

six billion pounds of goods, and they said of course that that situation is fraught with great danger because it is one of the greatest pressures towards inflation. I think at the present time that truths like this are needed to be told and understood. There is no question in my mind that we are in for a difficult period. There is no question in my mind that people have got to understand that there has to be forbearance, that if everyone rushes off without delay seeking what seems his own immediate interest the common interest may be so greatly injured that the interests of every one of us may be injured. I think what we need is a great deal of wholesome telling of the truth in a way that people can understand it. We are not in an easy position. The minister was very frank to say that. He has protected his position. He has given us really a very fair position except for this, that he has left us with this picture of wonderful progress. He has left us on the whole with the feeling that everything is good, and that if it is not good there is nothing we can do about it. Because, mark you, while the minister outlined these difficulties, and in particular said that if things went bad in the United States that would be very serious for us here, as it will, nevertheless if things go bad in the United States there will be a lot of things here that we shall have to try to do and we should be trying to prepare ourselves for that now.
I want to say a word about this question of prices. It is so full of importance and so full of difficulty. Let me take a case that is before us right now, one that is in everyone's mind because it happened no longer than within a day or so of the minister's budget, and because it affects every household. Let me take the price of butter. The average price of butter from 1926 to 1929-some farmer correct me if I am wrong-was 44 cents. Then in the depression from 1935 to 1939 it went down to 28 cents, and in August 1939 it was 27 cents. I suppose there is not one of us who went through that depression who did not think what a dreadful thing it was that the farmers were getting only 27 cents. When I say one of us I mean people like us who are intelligent. There was no serious man who was not troubled about the fact that the farmer was getting so little, and who did not want to find a way for the farmer to get more, and who did not realize that an improvement in the farmer's position would improve the position of all of us. Well, very good. The farmer was getting 27 cents in August 1939, and gradually during the war the price was allowed up to 45 cents, which I suppose was

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
little if any more than the cost. Bear in mind, if you go back to 1926-29 the price was 44 cents then.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How do 1929 and 1935 compare?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I told you. I said the price was 28 cents in 1935.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And between 1929 and 1935?

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will just go back to this. The price in the reasonably good years was 44 cents. It came down to 27 cents in 1939. During the war it went up to 45 cents, which was the price it had been away back in 1926, and now it has been increased. Some people talk as if the end of the world had come. Why is that? It is not because these people are unreasonable. It is because they have been deluded. It is because they have somehow or other got the idea that wages could go up and that other prices could be maintained indefinitely. The fortunate thing is-and this is what the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) has been saying for many months-that butter production is now beginning to increase, and we may have the better situation which we have been waiting for so long.
I want to end this by making this point. We need I think a great deal of wholesome plain truth-telling from those in authority so that there shall at the present time be the maximum self-restraint, self-control, mutual understanding, unwillingness to believe that every other man in the community is a crook. The place to get that from is in wise and considered statements from those in authority.
I would like to turn for a moment to deal with the three bases of our economic position as it is. I suppose it would be fair to say that the three main bases are: first, government expenditures; second, foreign trade, and third, the improvements and extensions being made by individual companies.
As to government expenditures I shall say nothing. That has been dealt with. We know that this year they will be less than last, but they will still be substantial.
As to foreign trade, all I wish to say at the moment is that there we have a situation which has been painted for us so clearly many times, and that is one of the reasons why I feel so regretful that the Minister of Finance has done nothing to consider the situation of business, the situation which has been painted so many times so clearly, and recently by the governor of the Bank of Canada. Much of our foreign trade is made possible only by the fact that we lend the money.
I wish to say a word about improvements and extensions, because this item is astonish-83166-179
ingly large, and I think it is well for us to dwell on it. It is well for us to dwell on it for a moment, particularly because of some observations that were made in the house some weeks ago by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). The figure for improvements and extensions during the current year is $1,700 million, a staggering sum, much the largest on record. In the low point of the depression I believe the corresponding sum was only $200 million. In 1929 I believe it was $1,100 million and it was the same in 1945. Here we have a record of $1,700 million. Most of that comes from where? Most of it comes from profit. It is desirable for us to know that. I took occasion to check up to make sure whether most of these amounts would be made up of bank loans, and I was assured it was not. The great bulk of it would be made up of profits, from the accumulation of companies themselves. I want to point out what an enormous work that is doing; and that leads me to say just a word about the question of profits.
In the house some weeks ago the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar mentioned quite a list of profits, many of them large. I hope I do not do him an injustice, but if my memory serves me rightly, when he gave these profits he practically said, isn't that terrible? He did not ask whether fair prices had been charged; he did not ask whether fair wages had been paid; he did not ask whether moderate dividends had been paid; he did not ask whether this money was available, as we know it is, for the most useful social services that oan be given. I do not believe that these points were absent from the mind of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, but I fear he felt it was enough for him to say that there were large profits and that that wias what interested a great many people. I suggest to him that if he finds that the prices and the wages are fair and that there are no inordinate dividends-^and he can satisfy himself on that -then these profits are a perfectly social thing, and that as we see it now, they are being used in a most social way.
I wish to say a word' about these companies' expenditures. No one will agree more readily than the minister-and he has already stated it-on how vital they are for our well being in this very year; how vital it is that the confidence, the courage and the readiness to take risks which impels people to launch out the vast sums, shall continue. He will agree that if want of confidence should arise, if the situation should change, it would be a very serious thing indeed. Therefore I find myself regretting very much two things: first of all the excess profits tax was not done away with.

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell

I would not have dared to say that in the house eighteen months ago, but I hope I have been here long enough, whatever people may think of my opinion, that they now believe I express at any rate my own opinion and do not speak for anyone else. I just wish to say this about the excess profits tax. I am all in favour of corporations being taxed, but I believe they should be taxed intelligently. The former Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) spoke stronglj- about the excess profits tax in the beginning of 1945. The present Minister of Finance did nothing to show that he disagreed with him, and yet that tax, I regret to admit, induces people sometimes to hold back when they should not. It has a tendency to induce business to carry on business in a bad way, in an inefficient way, in an extravagant way. There is no reason that I can see for continuing it. It just seems to me as though no one was ready to make a decision.
The second thing I want to say is that I think it is the greatest pity in the world that nothing is done in this country to try to encourage new industry, new enterprises. I was surprised to learn not so long ago that in the United States they gave advantages, preferences to new industries to a considerable amount-I believe as high as 38 per cent in taxation so that they can get on their feet. Those of us who believe in free enterprise must believe that, the very cornerstone of it is that new enterprise must come in; that it must correct the balance; that it must provide competition; that it must be the balance wheel which prevents the evils which my friends to the left often speak about, and that difficulties sometimes exist.

speechtext: Always.

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, not always; we would not be here if they existed always.
I wish to say just a word about the method of tax collection. We have heard about that for some time, and I think we are growing disappointed that so little is done. The other day I took occasion to call up a friend who has a great deal to do with tax collection, and I said to him: "Is it just as bad as ever?" He said: "Yes, practically as bad as ever." He said: "Of course, it is not the fault of the department; it is the fault of the law". I was relieved to hear the minister say the other day that a new act was on the way. I was relieved to see that he was taking time off to look at it himself, because he is an expert and an experienced man; but it is only one of the many things he has to do. I believe it is

so urgent to get it done that I hope at last it will be shoved along and that we shall have no more dilly-dallying with it.
I am not going to say anything today about economy. I hope and believe that some of my colleagues will fill up the gaps in my speech. I just wish to say that I think it is terribly hard, when one has been spending billions, to get down to mere millions, and when one has been spending millions to get down to mere thousands. I shall not do more than mention the classic remark of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), made to myself, incidentally: "Oh, yes, we may have saved a million, but what is that?" or words to that effect. I was struck by the speech made by the present Minister of Finance a year ago in connection with the budget, in which he laid a great deal of stress on the fact that members of the opposition had been a little irresponsible in asking for expenditures. I would refer him to the third chapter of Genesis where he will find words to this effect, "The woman tempted me and I did eat." Speaking seriously, I would say that the government is the government and we here after all can only bat things up to them. They have to make the decision. But I was disappointed, because I have always regarded him as a very serious man, with the remark made in this house last summer by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) in his reply on the budget speech. If I remember correctly, after referring almost with contempt, I must say, to various suggestions which had been made on this side for economy, which he characterized as rather unworthy of serious consideration, he then said, "Well, we will have to try to think up something ourselves." I thought that was late. The estimates were down-I am not sure whether the supplementaries were down -and it seemed to me to show an attitude towards this question which is not likely to produce the results that we want.
I want to say a word about inflation, just a word dealing wholly with the question of money supply. The minister did not deal with that, and in a way I was sorry that he did not because I think it is important. I think it is important for us to remember that the means of payment in the hands of the public, that is to say, the money or its equivalent which people have in their hands, is two and a half times what it was in 1939. It was then $2,400 million and now it is $7 billion. I would urge strongly that that huge amount should be reduced, and incidentally I am glad to see the minister the other day began a measure of reduction by partly pa}dng off a maturing loan

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
out of the government's own resources. I will not say more about that, particularly as I see that my time is running on.
I want to say a word about the whole question of easy money policy and I want to connect it with the question of interest rates. I also want to connect that particularly with ' that middle class that I spoke of a while ago, because in my opinion the existence of a strong middle class is vital and I believe the existence of a strong middle class is imperilled and perhaps made almost impossible by the conditions of today. I will not spend more than a minute in recalling to your minds what has happened to those countries where either they had no middle class or where the middlle class disappeared.
Let me say that by middle class I mean people, neither rich nor poor, who have a great desire to look after themselves, to provide for their present and for their future, and to be beholden to nobody, not even the state. They used to be regarded without question as the backbone of the community. They existed , only to a very small extent in Russia, and_that was why revolution could so easily- make itself felt and control Russia. The middle class used to be strong in Germany. We can remember when before the first great war the socialists were strong. They were not socialists in the modern sense; perhaps they would be called radicals or leftists; nevertheless they were strong and they had an influence. But they disappeared. There was inflation first of all in 1924 and then around 1931, and then finally in Hitler's day they were wiped out and that made possible this terrible abortion of the constitution, the terrible abortion of human relationships which prevailed in Germany.
For that reason I say that I believe the preservation of a strong middle class is important not merely economically but as going down to the very roots of our political being. What is happening to the middle class at present? Let us compare them with, say, fifty years ago. I think three things have happened. First of all of course costs have gone up; secondly, to a considerable extent, payment by special effort has become less common and they have not been able relatively to make the same wages; thirdly, the rate of interest has struck them. Fifty years ago the man who retired with a modest competency could get five or six per cent on it and he could reckon on living the rest of his life upon the proceeds. What happens today when he receives three per cent? And he is lucky if he gets that.
83166-179J
I believe that when we are considering this matter of the low-interest rate policy-and I know it is difficult, though it is attractive from the government's point of view-when, I say, we are considering this low-interest rate policy I suggest that this very important factor be taken into consideration-it is very important indeed-that there are large elements in the community who are suffering greatly by that policy. One other thing I would like to say in this connection. I would ask whether we can go on freeing other things and leaving the rate of interest tied down tight. Personally I very much doubt it and I think it is a matter worthy of the most serious consideration.
I want to say a word about the United States exchange. I thought the minister dealt with that in rather an airy fashion. He did say that we had suffered a loss of resources of some $600 million, but he pointed out, what is true enough, that that is because we were prosperous and had to import a lot. Nevertheless the fact is that our resources were greatly depleted. Then he went on to say, and this surprised me: "Well, if it gets difficult, after all we had a difficult situation in 1942 and we took some quiet, effective measures then"- as much as to say, "We will deal with the situation now in the same way."
Well, let us look at 1942. Although there was wisdom on our part, it was not our unaided wisdom in 1942 that dealt with the situation. The truth is that in 1942 the war dealt with it; the needs of the United States dealt with it. We remember very well that in 1942 the United States had need of many things from us. We for example had skills in war manufacture which they did not have at all. We were ahead of them in radar and in this and that, and for us to look with equanimity upon this situation now and bring in 1942 as a parallel is to me not dealing with the matter at all.
Finally I was disturbed with a remark which is attributed in the press to the governor of the Bank of Canada. I want to be very careful on this because it was only in the press and I think it may have been an offhand remark. I would not take it too seriously, but the governor was quoted as saying that it would be to our advantage-this is in connection with the whole question of exchange-if the price of gold were increased in the United States. That disturbed me very much because, I suppose, there could not be a more inflationary measure and because it seemed to me that if that was the only way, or was one of the serious ways, which the government regarded as a possibility of dealing
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell

with this thing, or of finding a way out, then it seemed to me the matter was not being dealt with as it should. Of course we all know that the final solution of exchange is trade, and I think we all agree, with reservations-I mean reservations in that we do not give up what we have until there is something better-that what we need is multilateral trade. But I call attention to the fact that even in our own cabinet we seem to have very great disagreement on that point. We 'have the Department of Finance in favour of multilateral trade, but apparently we have the Department of Agriculture absolutely against it, because whatever can be said for or against the bulk agreements with Britain, certainly they are not in accordance with multilateral trade. Certainly they are going to make it difficult; and incidentally it is highly open to question whether it was necessary for us to sell all the wheat to Britain at such a low price and whether we needed to entirely let out the United States from carrying some of the load.
So, Mr. Speaker, I would say that to me this budget, in spite of its sunshine features, is disappointing. It is a kind of wait and see budget, a kind of do nothing budget; yet before the year is out there may be a good many things that need to be done, and we may look back and regret that at least some of them were not done.
But the thing about which I complain most in this budget, the thing I wish to mention in closing, is this. I think of all the neglects of this budget by far the greatest is in respect of the field of dominion-provincial relations. I make no apology for coming back to this question, as I have done several times, because I believe not only that it is of vast importance but that somehow or other it is being relegated to a sphere far below that which it is entitled to . occupy. It seemed to me that the other night the minister spoke about the relations between the dominion and the provinces as you might speak about the relations between any group of eight or nine persons or institutions who had found it convenient to make a business arrangement with each other and who had carried on that arrangement as long as it was convenient, but who must be always ready to face the fact that perhaps they might not continue to find it very convenient to work along together. To me that is not only profoundly wrong; to me it attacks the very basis of our society. I should like to read, to the minister particularly, some words of a man who is often quoted. I understand he was a very dull speaker, and always emptied the House of Commons, but certainly he wrote well. I 
want to read these words, and as I do so perhaps some hon. members will be inclined first of all to say, "Well, that is just a lot of high falutin' sort of sermon stuff." I do not think it is, and later I shall say why I do not think so. This is Burke on society:
Society is indeed a contract. Subordinate contracts for objects of mere occasional interest may be dissolved at pleasure-but the state ought not to be considered as nothing better than a partnership agreement in a trade of pepper and coffee, calico or tobacco, or some other such low concern, to be taken up for a little temporary interest, and to be dissolved by the fancy of the parties. It is to be looked on with other reverence; because it is not a partnership in things subservient only to the gross animal existence of a temporary and perishable nature. It is a partnership in all science; a partnership in all art; a partnership in every virtue, and in all perfection. As the ends of such a partnership cannot be obtained in many generations, it becomes a partnership not only between those who are living, but between those who are living, those who are dead, and those who are to be horn. Each contract of each particular state is but a clause in the great primeval contract of eternal society, linking the lower with the higher natures, connecting the visible and invisible world, according to a fixed compact which holds all physical and all moral natures each in their appointed place.
Now I want to make the statement that if it were not that what I have read is a plain statement of fact, we would not be in this house today. It is only because those things are true, and practically true, and because there always have been enough men who lived up to them and made them true, that we are here today. Consider what is happening now. Here am I. an ordinary member of the opposition. I am able to stand up and express my views; I have just the same right, or almost the same right to speak as the Prime Minister has. Is that not a remarkable thing? Does that not mean this is a marvellous institution? What is the genius of our whole institution? It is the rights of minorities. Why, when we put pieces of paper in ballot boxes every five years, do we accept the verdict? Several times during the last twenty years I have not liked the verdict at all, but I have always obeyed it; and why? Because deep down I felt that the rights of the minority would be protected, that the minority would have a chance, and that this great institution built on these principles, spiritual principles and no others, would see to that; and that it was worth protecting, even though in the judgment of the electorate we had not been able to persuade them that we were right. Then take another thing; take the majesty of the law, on which we very often fail to reflect. Think of the majesty of the law; and I need not go further. I simply say that the principles I read to you

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
very briefly go to the very basis. They are practical. There is nothing illusory about them. We would not be here today; we would not be enjoying the prosperity we have today if it were not for the moral background which is behind this.
Now I want to read a short extract from a very different person, a brilliant man well known in this country, who died in his prime. I often think of what he might have done had he only lived. These are the words of D'Arcy McGee, speaking just before confederation :
Miracles would cease to he miracles if they were events of everyday occurrence; the very nature of wonders requires that they should be rare; and this is a miraculous and wonderful circumstance, that men at the head of the governments in five separate provinces, and men at the head of the parties opposing them, all agreed at the same time to sink party differences for the good of all, and did not shrink, at the risk of having their motives misunderstood, from associating together for the purpose of bringing about this result.
I have just one thing to add. I suppose we must admit there have been times within this last year when it would have been difficult to reconvene the dominion-provincial conference. It might have been suggested that on the part of one or other it was being done from weakness, that it was an act of appeasement, that somebody was going down on his knees to somebody else. But I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the present economy is free of all those difficulties. The governments have balanced their budgets. Tiles'- are out in the open. Nobody need take off his hat to anybody else. Everything is free and clear, and they can talk man to man.
But I do suggest this, that in this confederation nobody can suggest that things are happy at the present time. We have our difficulties. Here in the House of Commons we learn from each other-at least I hope we do. They have a saying in French, I believe, tout comprendre c'est tout pardonner. We learn to understand each other better here, and therefore we overcome our difficulties. But the difficulties are there. And it seems to me that every day that goes on, as things are now, the matter gets worse. Mark you this: things are well enough now, but of some of the difficulties outlined so clearly by the Minister of Finance should come upon us, let us say within the next six, nine or twelve months, we should need every ounce of strength that comes from standing shoulder to shoulder. And if this time should come, and we were not all together, the people of this country might well ask some questions. We have always
said-and everyone is guilty of this-that there are certain things which needed unity, which needed the action of all.
Here you have a family-and I am not forgetting the late Mr. Lapointe's saying that the dominion was not the father but, as I believe he said, the child of the provinces. I am not speaking constitutionally; I am just speaking in a human way. Here we have a family capable of working together, and yet we have at the present time the two eldest-

maintopic: THE BUDGET

speechtext:
My hon. friend knows his bible well, but sometimes wrongly. Here we have the two eldest who have grown up to be bigger and stronger than the others, but who want to play their part together-we have them for the present, I say, partly outside. Is it necessary that we should go on like that? I said the other day that a friend of mine had said that it was a scandal, and I do not know if that word is too strong. But I would say this, that it seems perfectly clear the initiative must come from the dominion.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), as was fit and proper, was the chairman of the conference. But I say again that if there are those who can recapture enough of that spirit-and it was a real spirit-which put this country together, and carried on through unbelievable difficulties, and if that spirit could be recaptured today, we would have a chance to get together, and to go along together, instead of as at the present time, hopelessly divided.
I wish to move the following amendment, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"This house regrets that the proposals of the Minister of Finance
(a)	offer no relief from the oppressive burden of indirect and hidden taxes on staple necessities that compose the family budget, all of which taxes directly increase the cost of living;
(b)	offer no encouragement to those engaged in the development of our natural resources, especially mining and agriculture;
(c)	fail to provide for reconvening the dominion-provincial conference in order to complete satisfactory agreements with the provinces and a dominion-provincial programme of social security, health and public investment."

maintopic: THE BUDGET
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) upon the great honour conferred upon him in his being selected to follow a distinguished line of ministers of finance and to introduce the annual budget. I was unable to be present
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

that evening, but I am told by my colleagues that the minister's speech was of a kind which followed well the traditions of his predecessors.
I wish to say, too, I am glad to see the hon. member from Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) back in his seat this afternoon, and able to act on behalf of the official opposition. I disagree with most of what he said, but I appreciate the contribution he makes to the debates of the house.
First let me make a comment on his criticism of my reference a few weeks ago to the profits that had been made in Canada over the past year. I had drawn attention to the largely increased profits made at a time when the costs of living were rising and the ordinary common man found it difficult to meet his obligations and to provide for his family. The figures I used on that occasion were, I believe, all from the Financial Post, although one or two may have been taken from some of the published reports in the Globe and Mail. I pointed out that one company showed an increase in profits for 1946 over 1945 of 309 per cent, that the Brack Silk Mills Limited showed an increase of 255 per cent. I admit I was wrong in one of my percentages, that dealing with Moirs Chocolate Company. I am glad to correct that this afternoon. The error was not my fault, but was due to a typographical error in the Financial Post. They gave a figure of $266,000 as profits, when the figure should have been $206,000. So I shall have to reduce the amount of profits which I gave, on a percentage basis, from an increase of 226 per cent down to 153 per cent.
But, Mr. Speaker, I still contend that even if the profits are used in the manner in which my hon. friend from Muskoka-Ontario says they are used, and not for the immediate payment of dividends, yet they are retained and added to the capital of these vast incorporations; so that after a period of time what actually happens is this, that the community has paid for the industry, and the shareholders own it. That is the effect of adding to capital from profits. May I point out that at the very outset of the war we urged the imposition of a capital gains tax. We foresaw large accumulations of capital in the war period, and prices and depreciation allowances were such that we contended it would be appropriate for the government to introduce a capital gains tax. Such a tax sooner or later will have to be considered by a successor to the present Minister of Finance.
I was particularly interested in the argument of the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario with regard to purchasing power. Hon. members will recall that he gave the amount of

circulating medium or money at the present time as $7,500 million or thereabouts, and suggested that this should be reduced-at a time when it is essential that our people shall have circulating medium in order to buy what we hope will be the additional products of peace time industry. It seems to me that that is going entirely the wrong way about the matter. As for interest rates, an increase of course would be satisfactory to the people who clip coupons and collect interest, but it would be most unsatisfactory to the hundreds of thousands of people who lack houses and other facilities and who would have to pay that interest. I am glad that the government intends to maintain the kind of cheap money policy that has been followed in this country for the past number of years.
I want to come now to a criticism of the budget from the point of view of this party. As I said, the minister made a remarkable speech, and he introduced a remarkable budget. Not only did he place before the house the results of the country's financial activities last year, the receipts and expenditures, but he showed in cold figures the effect of the great struggle we were lately engaged in and which not so long ago was brought to a victorious conclusion. The condensed estimated balance sheet of the dominion given by the minister to the house shows that on March 31 this year our net national debt had reached the colossal figure of $13,069,261,000. That is more than half the estimated value of the assets of every kind of all the people in Canada in 1927. The interest on this colossal debt is more than three times as large as it was before the war.
If we take the unmatured funded debt of Canada, which was given also in the table submitted to the house by the minister last week, of $16,524,161,000, we find that the interest obligation on that huge sum amounts to $437 million a year, or, as my recollection serves me, within $120 million of the total pre-war budget of this country. Thus apart from the sorrow and suffering occasioned by our losses in killed and wounded, we see what modern war entails in financial debt and interest obligations. May I take this opportunity of saying again that the lessons of this war should teach us that not only is war costly, but if we are to play our part to end the anarchy in international affairs which lies at the root of all war, we must be prepared not only to stand with the united nations against aggression wherever it may occur, but to do all in our power to remove, within as well as without our borders, the economic anarchy which produces war. Of course that this will

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
involve the nations in a surrender of a portion of their national sovereignty should not deter them from the task.
I think the budget was greeted with rather premature approval. The minister was able to make some statements which caught the public eye but which will not withstand close analysis. He was pleased that the government had entered the year with-and' I use his words-a surplus larger than the accumulated total of all previous surpluses in our history. I am going to join the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario in the criticism he made the night the budget was introduced of the large surplus of the financial year, but I shall do so from an entirely different standpoint. I question, not the amount but the manner in which this surplus was achieved.
The minister said that the total revenues for the year exceeded1 by S509 million the forecast made in the budget speech last year. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario said that we should not be grateful because the government took several hundred million dollars in taxes more than they needed to take. Neither the minister nor the financial critic of the opposition pointed out the real causes of this very large surplus, which I think in the main were two. First, there were the huge profits extracted from the people by industry and corporations, and which were reflected in the large increase in the proceeds from excess profits taxes and corporation income taxes. These accounted for the receipt of an additional $147,700,000. The second factor, however, I think is more important. I refer to the reduction or the elimination of subsidies on various consumer goods such as milk, edible oils, starch, sugar, beans, molasses, soap, tea, coffee, wool, cotton and other essentials which enter so largely into the cost of living of persons in the lowest income brackets. Some of these were removed only recently and did not affect it to any great extent, but the milk subsidy was removed last October. If profits had been curbed and the subsidies continued the surplus would have been far less.
In other words, the minister's surplus was achieved at the expense of every consumer in Canada, an expense falling most heavily on those least able to bear the burden. It is therefore not a matter which should invite congratulation, but on the contrary it should invite some condemnation. Incidentally this condemnation should be directed not only at the members of the government but at the members of the official opposition and such other hon. members who were persistent in their efforts to remove subsidies and controls.
Equally deceptive is the widely heralded approval of tax reductions. Newspapers last
Wednesday morning headlined their stories with such captions as, "Personal income tax slashed." They took the minister at his word when he said:
I am consequently proposing to make a substantial reduction of taxation in this budget. Moreover I am proposing to concentrate this reduction almost entirely in the field of personal income tax.
But did he do so? No. The total reduction in personal income tax is about $110 million, but the reduction in the excess profits tax of $279 million made in last year's budget, and the additional $10 million in this year's budget, make a total reduction of $289 million. Thus the estimated total excess profits tax for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1948, is $160 million as against $449 million for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1947.
Viewed in this light one can characterize the budget as a big business budget, which should satisfy our friends of the official opposition.
Nor will the reductions in personal income taxes bear very close scrutiny. The minister contended that the greatest proportion of relief was given to taxpayers in the low income brackets. He based his contention on what I think was a deceptive calculation, that of percentage reduction from the old tax levels. He said this:
The reduction as compared with present rates is as much as 54 per cent in the bottom bracket, but is limited to about 6 per cent or 7 per cent in the top brackets.
As a statement of fact, of course, that is quite true. Then the minister put on Hansard three tables of three different categories of taxpayers, comparing the new and old rates on the percentage basis. I have looked up the records and I cannot find when a similar percentage comparison was used before. On the contrary in some cases where there have been sharp increases or sharp decreases in personal income tax the amounts have usually been stated to the house in dollars. I am therefore going to ask permission of the house to table the same three categories of income taxpayers with the percentages given by the minister translated into dollars. May I have the permission of the house, Mr. Speaker, to do that?

speechtext:
The man with an income of $5,000, in the group for which the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario was making a plea just now, has a reduction more than fourteen times as great, and a man with an income of $10,000 a reduction more than thirty times as great as the man with the $1,000 income.
The minister said, that in making these reductions he wished to remove any serious barrier against a taxpayer working overtime. In our opinion the effective means to that end would have been to increase the exemptions to say $1,000 for a single man and $2,000 for a married man. Any objection that this would be reflected in the higher brackets, and of course objection would have been raised, could have been met by making the necessary adjustments in the graduated income tax. Increased exemptions, I might add, would have removed entirely, perhaps, in the case of the average working man, and almost entirely or at all events would have gone a long way towards meeting the criticism in the case of the farmer, doing away with what I consider to be entirely legitimate grievances.
Equally deceptive was the comparison between the proposed new Canadian personal income tax and the proposed new taxes in the United States. The minister's table is designed to support his contention that he is taxing the low groups in Canada less and the higher groups more than in the United States. That is incorrect, because be takes no account of the fact that in most of the states of the United States there is a state income tax as well as a federal income tax.

about that. I am simply expressing our point of view. We are not narrow nationalists, but we want Canada to occupy her proper place among the family of nations to which alone we are willing to allot certain aspects of our national sovereignty.
No; this budget does not do what the government would have us believe it does. The exemptions under the new budget are $750 for a single person, $1,500 for a married couple, and $1,700 for a couple with two children.
During the course of his argument the minister made *a significant statement which I should like to underline. He said, as reported at page 2554 of Hansard:
The exemption levels established last year are high enough to exempt completely from tax more than half the people earning incomes in Canada.
No doubt this statement was carefully checked by his advisers, but surely, Mr. Speaker, it is a sad commentary on the standard of living in this country, during the period of the highest national income that Canada has ever experienced. Indeed the minister expressed satisfaction because, as he said, as reported at page 2543 of Hansard:
Today we see a Canada enjoying a degree of prosperity never exceeded in living memory.
He commented:
We would appear to have ample excuse for self satisfaction and easy optimism if we took account only of our immediate situation here at home.
But the Toronto welfare council estimated that in 1944 a family of five required $1,864 a year in order to meet their bare living requirements. No frills were provided, no insurance, no allowance for health services, no provision for telephone, none for old age and so on-just the bare necessities of living. Since then, as I said a moment ago, the costs of living have risen sharply. The night before last I heard that the bureau of statistics had issued its recent figures showing that the cost of living jumped sharply in the month of March-not April, when a number of controls were removed, including rents-by 1-7 per cent, and that we w'ere now over 30 per cent higher in cost of living than the pre-war level. So that according to the minister more than half the people of Canada are living below a minimum standard. Where is the cause for easy optimism and self satisfaction of which he spoke? Where is the justification for sticking to the exemptions which were in effect last year? Indeed apparently the minister intends to profit by the increases in price level. Last
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

year he collected $298 million in sales tax. This year he expects to collect $325 million through the sales tax. Again let us remember that these bear most heavily upon those whose incomes are small, and like the tariff, the excise tax and so forth, they are hidden taxes; they are subjected to pyramiding as the articles pass from the wholesaler to the retailer, to the ultimate consumer and so on.
Then, too, the government is retaining the refundable portion of the income tax paid in former years. Food, clothing and shelter have risen sharply. Many families require these amounts now to meet the necessity of the purchase of houses, furniture, and clothing. To my',mind, the consumer, and indeed the small business man as well, could very well do with payment of these refundable amounts. I know that that would mean that the government would have to change the policy which it has laid down, but I think it would be justified in doing so. Because of what I have already said I wish to move a subamendment, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis):
That the following words be added to the amendment:
"(d) fail to raise the income tax exemption levels; and
(e) fail to make any provision for the more than half of our population who are compelled to live on incomes below the present exemption levels."
Indeed I find the budget speech in other respects somewhat illogical. The minister said, for example:
Had our taxes been raised gradually and under normal conditions to their present levels, had they been increased for the productive peacetime purposes of national development and social security rather than for the unproductive purposes of war, then the present levels might perhaps have been acceptable and tolerable as continuing levels.
The minister then argued that since the tax level had been raised for war purposes, it must be reduced. In other words the productive peacetime purposes of national development, well-being and social security must be secondary to the unproductive purposes of war. That is post-war defeatism which we must not accept. Indeed the minister warned that a recession might come-I put it mildly. This house should be concerned in maintaining those high levels of production, accompanied by a wide distribution of purchasing power, to ensure that depression will not come. The answer as to how higher standards of living can be secured is summed up in just two words, higher production. The major aim of the government's fiscal policy should be directed to maintaining and

enhancing the high levels to which the minister referred in such glowing terms. But the budget will not do this.
Another criticism I make of the budget is this. A modern budget must be more than merely a discussion of revenues and expenditures. Its financial proposals should form a part of an integrated national plan for increased production and the distribution of purchasing power among the people. Ever since the movement represented by this group was founded-and indeed long before that time-the men who represented labour and farmer parties in this house, the old Progressive party, the old Independent Labour party and so on, contended that what is physically possible is also financially possible. This, of course, depends upon intelligent planning for the increased production of goods, and their equitable distribution being regarded as the principal problem facing this nation. Upon its solution depends the maintenance of full employment and the level of agricultural returns. These depend again on spending. Spending is of two kinds, consumption spending and investment spending, spending for capital equipment. Consumption spending gives employment, while savings give employment only if they are invested for the purpose of capital equipment, such as factories, machines and so on. This is where conscious economic planning in the public interest becomes essential; for there is nothing under private enterprise which automatically maintains both types of expenditure at a sufficiently high level for prolonged periods to guarantee the maintenance of employment and of purchasing power.
Under private enterprise, decisions to save and to invest are made by different people at different times. If a boom develops, investment is high; but if a recession threatens, investment capital remains idle and after a while a depression follows. Obviously the state , can have very little control over the rate of saving of the individual under capitalism or indeed under any modern democratic system. Hence it is essential in a highly developed society like ours that there shall be a considerable control over investment if we are to maintain anything approaching a high level of employment. Indeed at times it will be necessary, we believe, for the state to supplement savings by financial operations through a publicly controlled financial system to maintain both a satisfactory rate of investment and purchasing power. But under our system of private enterprise and private banking there is no adequate machinery to direct

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
investment into desirable socially useful and effective channels. Indeed, no private agency could possess either the knowledge or the facilities to perform the task. Government reports all indicate that plans made by individual private businesses last year fell far short of their targets because they did not know the over-all picture concerning available supplies and so on. I venture to say that the statement tabled in the house this afternoon on behalf of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), giving an outline of the business possibilities for the coming year, will have exactly the same defect, because each individual planning does not know what the over-all picture of the economy is in which he plans.
The view that investment must be planned and controlled by public agencies is not peculiar to the C.C.F., nor is it peculiar to socialists. Lord Keynes in his book on the "General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money", said:
The duty of ordering the current volume of investment cannot safely be left in private hands.
This view was emphasized by Sir William Beveridge in his report to the British government several years ago on "Full Employment in a Free Society". Hence the modern budget should devote attention, and considerable attention, to the planning of investment, and this parliament should establish a national investment board to operate under a statute of parliament, defining its responsibilities and its powers.
Now obviously the control of investment cannot be effective without proper control of the banking system. The Bank of Canada under the present system can and does exercise some, if inadequate, control over the volume of credit, and that is a great gain over what we had some years ago. But the national central Bank of Canada can exercise no control over the direction of credit. This is in the hands of private chartered banks. They must be governed by the protection of the interest of their shareholders and, I do not think it is unfair to say, of the corporations and interests in which they, that is the banks or those who control them, have some interest. But lest someone should say that I am making a charge against directors of banks, may I say that there is nothing improper in their doing that-as long as the banks are private institutions. The Financial Post survey of corporate securities, and the directory of Canadian directors, show that 94 directors of three of the largest banks in Canada hold
between them some 800 directorships in 484 corporations and dozens of major industries. Included in the 800 directorships are 185 chairmanships or presidencies of companies, and knowing the conditions within the industries they direct, and being responsible for their success, they might be expected, to say the least, to be overcautious in financing the establishment or expansion of competitive enterprise.
Thus we believe that the banking, monetary and investment policies as well as taxation must be under the control of economic organizations responsible to the Canadian people through their elected representatives. The rules of the house preclude our moving for the socializing of the financial system. On February 3 of this year we sought to amend in this particular, the motion to adopt the address and approve the speech from the throne. The house did not then approve of our oft-repeated demand in the words we used calling for "the socialization of the financial institutions and monopolistic industries of the country" so that we could "plan the full and proper use of our natural resources and our currency and credit, in such a way as to provide full production and a rising standard of living for the Canadian people." That is what our amendment in February stated.
Events since then-this budget itself, and fears expressed by the minister and highly-placed economists and authorities, that a recession may come and come soon-emphasize the need for the policy outlined in our amendment to the address, and if the rules of the house permitted we would have moved it again today instead of what we have moved, although we believe that what we have moved is an important criticism of the budget policy.
In our opinion, then, the budget on the whole is disappointing, for it neither relieves the man in the lower brackets from burdens imposed by government policy and rising prices caused by removal of desirable controls and the abandonment of useful subsidies, nor indeed does it plan adequately for the future welfare of the Canadian people.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): I have listened with great interest to the two speeches that have been delivered this afternoon and I must say that with much of what both speakers have said I can agree. There were, of course, in each some things which I could not accept, but as the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) spoke I could imagine that if he remains long enough in the house he will become a pretty good social crediter. He is making real progress. There were a number of
The Budget-Mr. Low

things, which he said in a considerably better way than I could have said them, which reflected entirely the views which I take on a number of important problems that face Canadians at this time. I want to congratulate him and also to congratulate my hon. friend the member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Mac-donnell). It was unfortunate that the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario was not physically up to par today. I should like to have seen him in form, ready to tear into the budget, as I know he could very well have done had he been well.
With those words I should like to place squarely before the house the position of this group with respect to the budget. My first words must, of course, be words of sincere congratulation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on his maiden effort in presenting the budget. I believe everyone in the house enjoyed, as I know I did, his clear and rather jaunty but forceful presentation. In fact the minister had a way about him, an air of jovial, good-natured flexibility that carried us along in such a happy mood that we did not fully appreciate for some hours afterwards just what kind of medicine he was prescribing for members of the house and the people of the country. The minister's announcements of a huge surplus and of his income tax reductions were greeted with more real enthusiasm, I believe, than any budget announcements have received in a good many years.
But upon more sober reflection during the days following the presentation of the budget the enthusiasm of members of the house and of the people generally throughout this country subsided to a considerable extent. I believe most hon. members fully appreciate the indications in the budget of the strong present position of Canada and the highly satisfactory degree of stability with which we seem to have emerged from a disastrous war. Whether those indications are real or somewhat fancied will, of course, become apparent in the years to come, but I think the Minister of Finance has much reason for satisfaction in that he has been able to begin his career in the treasury department by bringing in one of the few balanced budgets Canada has had since confederation, and that he has been able to report at the outset of his experience that Canada's prestige is high throughout the world. It is only to be regretted that the retiring minister of finance (Mr. Ilsley) did not have that privilege after the burdensome war years during which he occupied that position.
I feel certain the minister himself realizes that, while he has been able to bring down a budget reflecting among other things Canada's 
strength, stability, balance and prestige, in reality we are at a most critical stage in the development of our country. There is no need for me to emphasize that the eyes of the world are on Canada, because our responsibilities in the world community of nations are very great indeed. We are poised in an in-between period. The war, with its strained activity, its restrictions, scarcities and lavish spending for destruction, is behind us, and we face an era in which our newly realized powers of production are seeking to be set free to make available a great abundance of much more diverse products than Canada has ever before known in her history. We are one of the remaining countries committed to a system of individual enterprise; and, though sometimes it appears that our commitment in that respect is something of a half-hearted, vacillating affair, nevertheless we are committed. And because that is so, the eyes of the world are upon us, some hoping we shall succeed in demonstrating to a confused world the superiority of that system, others hoping and planning that we shall fail utterly. That is why this is such a critical time. That is why people had every right to look for some evidence in this budget that the government is aware of our position and that it realizes the necessity of bold and sensible action to meet the needs of the challenging, dangerous time immediately ahead.
I do not wish to be pessimistic at all in my approach to a criticism of the budget. Actually I have great faith in our country and considerable optimism about its future. But when I think of what governments and finance ministers of the past eighty years have done to Canada I feel much as the old churchman felt when, in commenting upon the results of the missionary work his church had been doing, he was led to explain, "Surely God is with us, or these missionaries would have ruined the church a long time ago." I am sure Canada can achieve a glorious future, but if we are to realize that future I say that governments and finance ministers will have to repent immediately of the errors of commission and omission that have made waste of so much of our heritage.
