speechtext:
Yes, and listen to some of the prophets, but I do not see very many in front of me, particularly in the section occupied by the intruder.
As I view this budget, Mr. Speaker, I fail to see in it any tangible evidence that the government realizes the extremely critical nature of the times in which we are living.

The Budget-Mr. Low
Perhaps when the minister gives his rebuttal he will point out to us what things in the budget provide for a serious programme of conservation and an orderly development of our resources. Perhaps in his rebuttal he will tell us what there is in the budget to indicate any determination on the part of the government to do its part in keeping the gross national production high; what provisions in the budget reflect the government's determination to keep useful employment at a high level, at least a level high enough to guarantee widespread contentment on the part of the Canadian people; and what encouragement there is in the budget for business to expand to meet the pressing need for goods and services in this country. ' Thoughtful people are asking what there is in the budget to indicate that, as we advance into the period of mass production of consumer goods, the government will have in readiness a policy and machinery to maintain consumer purchasing power at a level sufficiently high to maintain a balanced economy^ These and many other questions are being asked by Canadians as they search this budget for signs upon which to base their hopes for the future.
In a general way, the budget is a whopping big $2,450 million baby. I must say that, buoyant as were the spirits of the minister when he presented it to us, he himself must have been aware that this offspring will take considerable nourishment from the Canadian people. The sum of $2,200 million is a large amount to lift from 3,000,000 families in one year, but $2,200 million is what the minister proposes to tax out of the Canadian people in 1947. This means that the average Canadian family will have to dig up over $700 in taxes during next year. The average Canadian family therefore wonders if it can carry that load and still meet its own needs in these times. Wearily most of them look ahead wondering if there is to be any substantial relief from the heavy burden they bore so patiently during the war. I commend them for their patient forbearance during that time.
The average taxpayer is to be congratulated on what he did during the war. Without complaining he met conditions as they arose, and he met them extremely well. But as our taxpayers strain to see into the future two facts stare them straight in the face. The first of these is this. It appears that the government has committed itself to yearly expenditures of around $2,000 million, a sum more than three times the budget of the last year before the war. The second fact is that the load can be borne only if the gross national production and Canada's business activity
remain at or very near their present high levels. These are sobering facts, to be sure, and no one will blame the Canadian taxpayers if they show some anxiety about the future. Even if this national production remains at over $11,000 million a year, we shall have to pay over to this government twenty per cent of that production in the form of taxes. .
At first glance the budget appears to have made sweeping reductions in the income tax rates. This phase the minister emphasized with such gusto that most of us were at first inclined to overlook the fact that he disappointed many thousands of Canadians by not raising the exemptions as they confidently expected him to do. Speaking for this group, we have always advocated the raising of the exemptions, and we will not relax our efforts in that respect. We still feel that these exemptions should have been raised and that more taxpayers in Canada should have been relieved entirely of the burden of taxes, particularly in the light of the fact that so many of our people, as has been pointed out already by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well) have been languishing on a standard of living away below what they should have had. One newspaper writer put it in this way: "It will be Liberal strategy, of course, to whoop up the size of the cuts in the income tax and to hush up the omission of reductions in sales and excise taxes." But let us take a look at the income tax reductions and see if they really are sweeping. I think hon. members will recall that a few weeks ago the Ottawa Citizen carried a budget for the married man living in Ottawa, and having a weekly income of $40. How would he fare under this budget? He will pay in 1947 the sum of $94, as compared with $118 under the old rates. He will save the huge sum of $24, or about forty-eight cents a week! His saving will be cold comfort in the light of the increase in the cost of his living which came at about, the time the budget was brought down.
This example gives a fair indication of what has been done to taxpayers generally. Let me hasten to say to the minister that he is to be congratulated upon framing his income tax proposals at least with a view to encouraging wage-earners who are in the middle brackets, and wishing to provide them with an incentive to higher earnings, and therefore a greater productive effort. Had the cost of living remained at pre-budget levels, the minister's action would have done much to settle labour generally. Reductions in their income tax would have been clear salary or wage increases,
2S14
The Budget-Mr. Low

as indeed they will be in the future when an abundance of consumer goods available will bring living costs down.
It will be much to the advantage of wage-earners, therefore, to hasten the day of lower consumer goods prices by maximum effort now to produce goods, so that the finance minister's promise for the next year might be made good. Labouring men and wage-earners generally are not likely soon to forget that the so-called tax relief for this year is only a gesture. About
2,000,000 wage-earners in Canada are fully conscious of the fact that this budget does not mean a single thing for them, except higher living costs for some months to come, a thing largely avoidable when one considers that another $100 million could have been taken off taxes in such a way as to reduce the cost of living, and without in any way endangering the financial stability of the government.
The minister is planning for a large surplus, anyway, a surplus much larger than he has any right to expect the Canadian people to be happy about, in the light of their present circumstances. It is my judgment that the government owes it to the Canadian people generally to tackle the problem of hidden and nuisance taxes, and to tackle that problem with earnestness and sincerity. That would indicate, it seems to me, whether or not the Liberal party is really interested in the common man-the little fellows-as they so often say they are.
The government proposes to take from Canadians this year $1,045 million in the form of indirect taxes, most of which are hidden or nuisance taxes. That means that around forty-seven per cent of all the tax revenue this year will represent feathers plucked from the goose in the so-called painless method. From the government's point of view there is, of course, something to be said for these indirect, hidden taxes. But from the point of view of the common man there is much more to be said for the removal of many of them at the earliest possible time. These are the taxes which are responsible for the increasing costs of production. They are applied at various stages of manufacture and the assembly of consumer and capital goods, so that they have a general pyramiding effect upon prices. The ultimate consumer is the goat who has to pay them. And it is mainly those taxes which have been responsible for the widening divergence between farmers' incomes and the cost to them of the many things which they have to buy.
I should say it would make a most interesting research problem, if one were to attempt to untangle the maze of hidden and indirect

tax applications to a selected list of common things bought every day by the people. But I will say this, that I have gone far enough into the matter to be convinced that it would be far from easy, and I am convinced it would take the skill of highly trained cost accountants to get anything like an accurate picture of the whole complicated mess; because that is just what it is, a complicated mess.
I have not the full facts before me, but one can get some idea of what is involved by taking cigarettes as an example. I am told that the actual legitimate cost involved in a package of cigarettes that sells for thirty-two cents is about eight cents. The remainder of twenty-four cents is pyramided taxes of a great many varieties. This may be an extreme example; it probably is.
I am not so much concerned about luxuries as I am about things we have to buy from day to day in order to live, but the example illustrates the general effect that hidden taxes have on consumer prices. Certainly the Minister of Finance could have performed a real service to the Canadian people by removing some of these taxes altogether, and by reducing others to a lower economic level. He could have taken off safely this year, in my estimation, $110 million of this particular tax burden; and, had he done so, the resulting possible decrease in living costs would have made his income tax rates reductions worth something to the Canadian consumer. Before I leave that may I say that it would have meant something tangible to the more than
2,000,000 wage-earners in this country who are not included in the benefits derived by the reduced income tax rates.
In this connection there is another angle which I should like briefly to mention. In my estimation the best barometer for measuring efficiency of government is the tax level, compared with the services that are being granted to the people for their money. People can readily measure the efficiency of their government only if their tax levels are easy to see, if they are right out in front of them, like a huge thermometer. But if the goose is to be plucked without knowing it is losing its feathers, or, in other words, if fully half our taxes are hidden ones that people cannot see, or cannot immediately discern, then Canadians can have no accurate way of telling whether or not their government is doing a decent job.
For this, and also for the reason that indirect taxes do add to the cost of production, the minister has utterly failed the Canadian people at .this time by not including in the budget provision for abolishing and/or lowering sales, excise and nuisance taxes. When the people

The Budget-Mr. Low
of Canada leam the true facts about our tax system, they will surely rise in righteous indignation, and put into office a government which will begin at once the simplification, and downward revision of the whole process of tax structure.
I should like to turn for a few moments to the matter of trade. In his speech the Minister of Finance made these two statements :
We now have reached the time when Canada may expect to benefit from the new international machinery which has been established during recent years 'to aid in international monetary and financial affairs.
And again he said:
Some of our largest customers are buying more from Canada, because of their abnormal needs at present, and because other normal sources of supply are not available, than we can reasonably expect them to buy on a continuing basis. We must be prepared for reductions in some or all of these abnormal expenditures of various types in the not-too-distant future, and we must be prepared for the changes and adjustments in our production necessary to fit it into a more permanent pattern.
With regard to the first statement, I shall content myself at this time by simply saying that I sincerely trust it is not merely an expression of a pious hope. At the time we ratified/ Canada's approval of the Bretton Woods agreement, I did not hear much, if anything, from the government about what action they were prepared1 to take to impress upon large creditor nations with which Canada does business that a high and satisfactory level of international trade must depend upon their willingness to accept imports of goods from us to pay for their exports of goods to us.
The government, as we have already pointed out, rushed into that agreement without stopping to consider the very high price that Canada is likely to have to pay for a very doubtful privilege. But, now that we are a party to this tax, our job is to use our influence on every possible occasion to drive home to our neighbour to the south, especially, her sacred responsibility in this whole matter of trade. I believe I am right when I say that to a very large extent the economic stability of nearly every country on the earth and the peace and security of the world depend upon the attitude of the United States of America toward' trade. Somehow the man on the street in that great country must come to understand how great that responsibility really is.
With regard to the second extract from the minister's speech I should like to say just a few words. Canada ought to prepare herself and her machinery right now to meet what the minister has forecast with respect to a reduced foreign demand for Canadian goods. Two
things are prominently in my mind about that matter at this time. The first is this. It stands to reason that as keener competition for markets develops throughout the world- and that will come sooner than many people expect-we in Canada will be forced to lower our cost of production of a good many things if we are to retain our markets abroad. Here again I contend is a strong argument for the complete overhaul of our taxation structure and for the abolition of much of our indirect taxation that adds to the cost of production. In my judgment it would be worse than shortsighted for us merely to wait and see what happens, as is so often the attitude adopted. The removal of these taxes now will help to put us in a much better competitive position later on when the need is upon us.
In the second place, we ought to be giving much attention to the local market. After all, only a comparatively small percentage of Canada's business is done with countries abroad. We ought to be turning our attention to the fullest possible satisfaction of our internal demand for the goods and services which we in Canada can produce. I do not mean by this to neglect our foreign trade. Far from it; let us expand it to the utmost without lowering the standard of living of the Canadian people; I emphasize that, without lowering the standard of living of the Canadian people.
That means, of course, balancing our exports with our imports. AVhat I have in mind is that when the time comes that the present abnormal demand for our products drops off abroad we should be well on our way to potential economic self-sufficiency in the essentials of living. I am sure that is the only safe position for Canada in the next fifteen years or so. We should take every precaution to see that if strikes or social upheavals in other countries or war interfere with our sources of supply our people will not suffer because we have neglected to develop our own resources at least to the extent that we could1 within reasonable time satisfy our own basic needs. I would have felt much better about the budget if I could have found in it some evidence that the government intends putting Canada into such a position at the earliest possible time.
It was gratifying to note from the minister's speech that he expects production in Canada during 1947 to reach $12,000 million at prices slightly higher than those prevailing in 1946. We may be fairly hopeful then that employment will continue at a high level during the year. It is most important that such be the case, for without a high level of income the people will not be able to pay the tre-
The Budget-Mr. Low

mendous volume of taxes required by the government to fulfil its commitments. In fact there can be no guarantee of real prosperity if we do not make possible the production of vast quantities of goods and their distribution to the masses of the Canadian people. I wonder if this government is facing up squarely to the problems associated with keeping production high. There is little in the budget to indicate its attitude in this respect.
Competent authorities estimate that it will require production to the value of approximately SI,000 a year per head of population if we are to maintain a high and satisfactory level of wage-earning employment. Investigation in the United States, where conditions are not very much different from our own, indicate that that country must produce not less than $170 billion worth of goods a year to reach anything like full employment. From that it would appear that in Canada we must maintain between $11 and $12 billion worth of production a year to do a similar job. Henry Kaiser recently made this statement:
If we fail to have full employment we will not only face national bankruptcy but a social upheaval in which the American democratic form of government might well be swept away.
I believe it is just that serious a matter. Now I do not like the term "full employment", because there is something about it which reminds me of Schikelgruber and his "full employment", but I do recognize the need of providing opportunities for useful employment with appropriate incomes for the vast majority of our people. I believe this calls for careful organization and for vision on the part of the leaders of this nation.
Many leading men in the United States have been studying the whole problem of employment, with its related problems of production, markets and maintenance of purchasing power at a level to balance with the production. The United States congress has recognized its responsibility in meeting the problem by passing the full employment bill. They are determined to provide jobs with pay to all Americans who wish to work. There is much evidence that leading thinkers in the United States now recognize that the major difficulty to overcome in any programme of high production and employment is that of maintaining consumer purchasing power at the point where the goods produced and the services offered can be taken off the market and consumed and used by the people.
Beardsley Ruml, about whom the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) spoke a few days ago, educator, social scientist and business executive, chairman of the board of R. H.

Macy, Incorporated, and a director of the national bureau of economic research in the United States, said recently in an article he wrote for Cosmopolitan magazine:
We were able to sell what we produced in 1946 as a result of four strong abnormal forces operating in 1946

reconversion spending, inventory building, net exports abroad, and lower government receipts than expenditures during most of the year. The forces that gave us full employment in 1946 will be weaker in 1947. And so we will have a weakening of the 1946 basis for full employment. The future must find the substitutes for the abnormal wrar and war conversion props to consumer purchasing power. Will they be found in 1947?
The production in 1946, to which he refers, in the United States was approximately $180,000 million. What Mr. Ruml said of his own country holds good here in Canada. There will be no use in thinking that pent-up wartime savings will prop up consumer demand. Mr. Ruml had something to say about this, too, and I quote:
There is no solace in a so-called pent-up demand. There has always been a pent-up demand, even at the lowest points of depression. The question is not demand, but effective demand. Our economic reconversion must be to find a peace-time substitute for those non-recurring strong forces which were the legacy of war and post-war disorder.
rft is the quantity of money in the pockets to buy that makes employment. Our biggest job in the future will be to maintain that kind of purchasing power at a level high enough to ensure the distribution of our whole production. If we fail in that, our way of life, our freedom, the individual system of responsible enterprise are all doomed. There are a great many people thinking in just those terms today. Take a look at what Harper's magazine crack writer John Fischer has to say, as reported by Richard L. Strout:
Russians are seared by their cast-iron Marxist logic about American capitalism. No amount of argument will shake their doctrinaire belief that American capitalism will produce a major depression in the next fifteen years, that this will produce fascism, and that this will produce war.
He continues:
Thus if there isn't a depression in the next fifteen years, the Russians might change their *tune. Facts will speak louder than words. From all this it can be argued that one way to preserve international peace in the world is to prevent that depression which the Russians believe will lead to war.
That argument applies equally to the widely-held opposite thesis that Russia is hoping for a major depression in the United States, with the consequent weakening of American economic and political power abroad, paving the way for further Russian expansion and influence. Thus a healthy American economy and wise trade policy are considered imperative checks to the spread of communism.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise this afternoon to ask you for the privilege of the floor and to address this august assembly I assure you that I shall present my own thoughts, not written and rewritten and corrected, but the sincere beliefs that I hold myself, which possibly may not make as fine reading as the impeccable language we have heard this afternoon, but will, I repeat, be my own thoughts and those, I believe, of the majority of the people of the great province from which I come.
As I enter the arena this afternoon I do not do so with the thought of breaking a lance with the redoubtable warriors who have already entered it. I wish only to help the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and this Canada of ours by once more pointing out to him and to the hon. gentlemen of this assembly the tremendous possibilities of the resources of Alberta which I am going to ask all hon. members to help develop.
Some of the statements made by speakers who have preceded me struck me as requiring some answer; but, having recently sustained an injury which has compelled me to be quiet and from which I am not yet fully recovered, I thought my duty would be better fulfilled were I to speak only of the things I mentioned at the outset.
Lately the Imperial Oil Company has made a great discovery of oil. I am not boosting the Imperial Oil Company; I am simply reciting a fact. They have discovered one of the most important oil wells ever found in Alberta, a few miles south of the city of Edmonton, near the town of Leduc. Many times in this house I, as member for Athabaska, have tried to impress the people of this country with the possibilities of the tar sands of that great Athabaska region. I have said to the doubting Thomases of eastern Canada that over there lie resources which are so vast and so immense as to stagger the imagination and which could make this Canada of ours, in spite of the doubts expressed in this budget debate so far, one of the wealthiest and most self-contained countries in the world.
First I mention oil, then gas and coal. No nation can be powerful in time of war and rich and prosperous in time of peace unless it has a plentiful supply of these resources. We all know but often forget that Alberta possesses more coal, lignite, bituminous, semi-bituminous and semi-anthracite, than all the rest of the provinces put together, and that they constitute a large percentage of the coal
The Budget-Mr. Dechene

resources of the British empire. I do not overlook the fact, and I hope nobody does, that a shortage of this material, without which no nation can be great and powerful, may develop. Experts in the United States are predicting today a shorter life for the oil resources of that country than for Canada's. Lignite was used by the Germans for years as a source of oil and gas. In the tar sands of McMurray and along the great Athabaska river are hundreds of millions, yes, billions of barrels of potential oil if we Canadians would only use the talents and the courage that we have in this country and show the same adventurous spirit of our ancestors who centuries ago were drawn there by the appeal of this great western country. I say to the Minister of Finance, who presented such a wonderful budget, cheerful and able, that if we develop the resources of Alberta alone, in a few years, in a few decades at most, the Minister of Finance can close his books and not worry about surpluses or meeting the obligations of Canada.
Some hon. members listening to me today may doubt the incredible, the staggering resources we have in that province which today has a population of less than the city of Montreal. That population may be only
800,000,	but what a great population it is, what a population of pioneers! When I was a young fellow in the Edmonton district with my father, who homesteaded some twenty-five miles north of that city nearly sixty years ago, we had confidence in that country; we bad confidence in ourselves. Some years later, in the legislature of Alberta as well as in the House of Commons of Canada, this country of youth, I was astounded and sorrowed by the expressions of doubts, of despair even, of the future of that great county and particularly of the possibilities of Alberta. I am now, sir, walking in the shadow of life, but I still have the spirit and the courage of youth, and I use my voice to the best of my ability to boost Alberta.
In 1922, on the floor of the legislature of Alberta I predicted that under the soil of the province-and may I say that that soil is good enough for anything; its fecundity is beyond comparison-there was the wealth of which I have spoken, immense resources of oil and of all minerals; but I was made the butt of jokes when I asked the province of Alberta to pay a bonus of from 850,000 to 8100,000 to the first company or individual that would find this oil and bring in a producing well of at least 1,000 barrels a day. How they laughed at me! Today, Mr. Speaker, the work has been done and the field has been proved. At that time I deplored and I still deplore the fact

that our public men, the provincial government as well as the federal government, never saw fit to retain to the holders of the topsoil the natural resources underneath. When a homesteader went out west, thirty, forty or fifty years ago and gave everything he bad, gave his health, his brawn and his courage in order to develop that great western country our government, if you please, saw fit, I suppose for the sake of the large corporations now benefiting by their development, when they gave title to the homesteader, to give him title to the surface only. He could cut the trees, pull the stumps, take out the stones and through that labour break his heart and his back in developing that great country, but if there was a million dollars under it, it went to somebody else; he had no right to it.

I have seen hundreds of these people going through my own town with broken-down hay racks and wagons, their horses played out, with a cow or two, which they had somehow or another saved from starvation, lagging behind because they were too weak to keep up with the procession. But these people had one thing left. They had the courage and the guts to move hundreds of miles to the north country, and there they are now. Let us give them those lines which they have been depending upon in order that the fruits of their toil and of their courage, seeing that they have started life twice over, so to speak, shall not be lost to them.
I do not know what politics has in store for me, and that is not very important. The fate of an ordinary man in politics is of no consequence; it is only a drop in the bucket, and as a man gets older it is worth still less to him. But I should like to live long enough to be able to tell those people, whose sacrifices I have witnessed, to whose courage I can testify, that the transportation facilities which we promised them have been built by the country.
I am making this plea tonight for those people and, I repeat, I am not asking a favour. I am not asking for anything on bended knee, or hat in hand, because we never do that in that country. I do not very often ask for the privilege of holding the floor, Mr. Speaker, and this is the first time I am speaking this session, so that I am sure you will bear with me as I tell the story of the people in that part of Canada. Some weeks ago, over in the Chateau Laurier, one of the engineers of the Department of Mines and Resources presented a report on the new findings in the Fort McMurray field, some twenty or twenty-five miles west of the location where we had been working in connection with the Abasand oil. In that district they found clear lakes of bitumen. Anyone who wishes to inspect them can see the plans in the department which the engineers brought back and the description of the lakes containing bitumen to a considerable depth ready to lay on the roads of the country to make pavements. These lakes, according to the chief engineer, who is one of the best in the country-I do

not suppose I need to mention his name- have a capacity of 500,000,000 barrels of bitumen; something simply staggering. To those hon. gentlemen from eastern Canada these figures may appear incredible, but they are not so to the people in that part of the country. We have heard farmers talking about yields of from fifty thousand to sixty thousand bushels of wheat, and that is not a dream; it is true. Well, if you operate on fifty acres and you lose your crop you can get by; but when you operate on an area of a thousand or two or three thousand acres, failure means a very great deal to you. That is why our farmers are so greatly interested in the prices of twine, gas and everything else. I suggest to hon. gentlemen that they should not criticize the farmers too severely if the latter seem to be bitter at times, because they have to operate on such an extensive scale that it is a tremendously expensive business to them, and if we do not help them to secure the instruments of production as cheaply as possible, we cannot be surprised if they complain.
May I ask. Mr. Speaker, that you call it six o'clock. I had hoped to be able to complete my remarks before the dinner hour, but I have taken only twenty minutes and I should like to speak for the other twenty minutes this evening.

Mr. Chairman, as I am the representative for the constituency in which this railroad is to be built, I believe I should say a few words on section 7, especially in view of the amazing contentions introduced into the discussion recently by some hon. members. I should like to say, first of all, that, notwithstanding the wishes of certain individuals there are still in Canada provinces which have their rights and powers, and it seems to me that it might as well be said once and for all that no one can foresee the day when there will be only one central power in Canada. If any such thing should ever happen, the confederation would be broken altogether.
As has been already said by the hon. member for Outremont, section 7 deals exclusively with the right to build a railroad. It has not anything to do with mining development. According to paragraph 5 of section 92 of the British North America Act, each provincial legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to matters comihg within the class of subjects therein enumerated; and paragraph 5 refers to the management and sale of the public lands belonging to the province and of the timber and wood thereon.
Then, if we want to know what are the public lands belonging to the provinces we must refer to section 117 of the British North America Act, which states:
The several provinces shall retain all their respective public property not otherwise disposed of in this act, subject to the right of Canada to assume any lands or public property required for fortification or for the defence of [DOT]the country.

And we must also refer to sections 108 and 109, which state that in matters such as this the provincial governments have the absolute right to dispose of the lands, and to grant permits to mining corporations.
In virtue of the powers thus given, 'the legislature of Quebec passed a law in 1946, which is set out as chapter 42, 10 George VI, of the statutes for that province. This measure is entitled, "an Act to promote mining and industrial development within New Quebec. In sections 1 and 2 it is stated:
1. The minister of mines-
That is the provincial minister.
-is authorized to grant to Hollinger North Shore Exploration Company Limited, in replacement of the special licence number 4676 which it presently holds, a special exploration licence under conditions specified in-

the following sections.
And in section 2 of the same act it is stated:
This licence shall be issued for a period of time running from the date of its issue until June 30, 1952.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, it is entirely out of order to discuss in this chamber the granting to the Hollinger company of the necessary permit for the exploitation of the mining fields in that area. That must be taken as a fait accompli; and the only question is this: Is this parliament to give to another company the right to build a railroad to facilitate the exploitation of these mining fields? Therefore I am entirely in favour of the principle of the bill, and I shall support section 7.

Looking back over the history of this country, one realizes that similar rights have been granted without full information and without guarantees as to what was to be done with these rights. In many instances this has resulted in restricting the development of the country.
I was a member of the committee which dealt with this bill and gave it serious consideration. This is an important matter, but no record was kept of the proceedings of that committee. Mr. Chairman, I think I have the right to illustrate what happened years ago, and what may happen again in the future.
This is a most important matter. As I pointed out before, there was no verbatim report of the committee proceedings, and the sponsor of the bill has not given a complete and elaborate statement to this committee. If I am permitted to do so I am going to present some facts as to what has happened in the past, to illustrate that this very same procedure in the past has worked to the detriment of many Canadian people, and to the detriment of the development of Canada.
Hundreds of those people, many of them without any substantial means, sweat out years of their lives in developing those properties. The owners who purchased from the government guaranteed certain rights and also guaranteed certain road developments. Those developments did not happen. Why? Because at that time they were not tied down. They made a verbal bargain, and had made certain promises in their literature. The government of the day had nothing concrete from which they could work to keep those people to their agreements.
That is why I object to this bill, without knowing more about these proposals. I have before me a book called "The History of Canadian Wealth," by Myers, a volume I would recommend to hon. members who are interested in the development of Canada. They will get it in the parliamentary library, and I recommend that they read it, because it gives dozens of illustrations of what happened in the past in connection with the development of this country. I am just going to read the preface before going on with my argument. It reads:
The rapid concentration of wealth in Canada is no mere fancy. Already, it is estimated, less than fifty men control $4,000,000,000, or more than one-third of Canada's material wealth as expressed in railways, banks, factories, mines, land and other properties and resources.
To say that this small group of individuals control so vast a wealth and the agencies of its production does not imply that they own it all. Between ownership and control there is a difference, yet the reverse of that is commonly supposed. By means of their control of financial markets and distributive systems, a small number of men may effectively control sources of wealth which still may remain under individual ownership, as witness the case of the farms, of which control farmers throughout Canada are bitterly complaining.
