Mr. Speaker, it is with deep regret that I admit I could not complete my remarks before six o'clock and that therefore I must inflict myself upon you for a few minutes longer. I believe that in my style -as you notice, I have nothing written before me-and being in the habit of saying what I think and talking about things I am supposed to know something about, I have made a point as to the necessity of this government and the government of Alberta coming to a thorough understanding of the immense possibilities in the development of the tremendous natural resources of that province, which I discussed for a few minutes. I know that this time will not be lost.
Some time ago I was reading one of the greatest writers and thinkers of his century, Victor Hugo, and I was struck with one statement he made at a time when things were most desperate for his great country, France, as bad almost as they were in the' last war. I speak of 1871, and I would ask for a minute of your time to refer to those days, because at that moment everything seemed to be lost. The country was absolutely defeated; its armies were dispersed over the soil of France; the conquerors were tramping through the halls of the nation with their hobnailed boots, imposing harsh terms of peace. Hugo was himself a member of the chamber of deputies, which met under the walls while the commune was burning the city. Everything seemed desperate; they said, "Well, what is the use?" Then Hugo uttered these words: "Gentlemen, no effort is ever lost." You all
know how true that is. Sometimes you have wondered what is the use of what you are trying to do. I see around me young members, men of talent, ability and courage, who one day are going to make their mark in this chamber where I am so proud to be tonight. Sometimes they will be inclined to be discouraged and to ask, "What is the use?" If they remain true to the cause they espouse; if they keep pressing forward they will find later, when perhaps they think their ideas have been forgotten, that their efforts have not been lost. Therefore tonight I repeat that celebrated phrase, which I am unable to translate: "Fut-on un million d'esclaves, je suis fibre." It is because I know I am appealing to a friendly house, because I feel that I am appealing to real Canadians, because I know, as I said a moment ago, that tnese efforts will not be lost, that I am asking the house to consider building the gaps in these railroads about which I have spoken so often. I say again that if the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are unable to complete the gaps on their fine because they must produce profits for the shareholders, we have the right here to cancel the charter they obtained in what, after all, was Canadian National territory. They were granted these charters away back in the boom years of 1927, 1928 and 1929 because even then they could see the tremendous possibilities of that great northland, which knows no crop failure.
I remember in 1937, when Saskatchewan suffered drought, hearing a man express the view that Saskatchewan was done. What an awful thing to say! W'hy, we have only started in the west. We are only beginning; and all we are asking you, through my feeble voice as member for one of the largest ridings in this dominion, is to lend us your help so that the development of that great western country may be carried out as promptly as possible. The province of Alberta cannot by itself construct the highways and railroads that are needed. For instance, they are unable to construct the highway from Fort McMurray to Edmonton which would make available those great tar resources of which I was speaking this afternoon.
If I had time I should like to say a word about another resource.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go ahead.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My voice is giving out. I know [DOT]what I am about to say will sound like heresy to my good friends from the east and west coasts, but I say quite sincerely that the greatest fish in the world, bar none, do not come from our coastal fisheries but from our northern lakes. I have in my constituency
The Budget-Mr. Dechene

Cold lake, where we catch trout at depths of three and four hundred feet. They are so good, so incomparable that we find it hard to get any for our own use, because the Chicago and New York markets will take every fish they can possibly get from that part of the country. In that connection hatcheries should be built. I maj' be told that this is a provincial matter, but that is not entirely the case. We must work this thing out together.
Having said so much, let me say this. I would not speak in this way if I did not have confidence in this government and in the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I know that all of us, no matter what may be our political affiliations, are proud of the tremendous job done by the former Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) during the war. I met him on a street-car one day after a difficult evening during one of the most sombre, terrible years of the war, when he was being criticized not only from across the way but right from this side of the house by some very able men. If I tell this incident I know you will all appreciate it. He said to me, "I hope I am doing the right thing; that is all I worry about, doing what is right." He went on to say, "Those two men may drive me out of political life, but if they do I will go down with the feeling that I have done my duty to my country in its years of struggle and peril." I said to the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, "Your name will stand high. It will be remembered in the schools of this land when those other men have been absolutely forgotten." And in his successor I salute one of the ablest young men in the political life of this country. Under the former Minister of Finance the bonds of the province of Alberta were redeemed, so that today our credit is 100 per cent. I know when the province of Alberta comes to the present minister it will be received as that province and its people ought and deserve to be received.
I will not keep the house any longer. I regret having inflicted myself upon you; but since I have a few minutes left I should like to describe northern Alberta in June. Let us go home for June. Then the wild roses grow rank along the highways. Their aroma is the first thing that strikes a stranger. They grow almost like trees, and they are the colour of the cheeks of our girls and women. There is nothing more beautiful than northern Alberta in June, nothing lovelier than a northern Alberta June bride. Now. in spite of a late spring, our farmers are on the land. They may crab about the price of gas, the price of twine, the price of this and the price of that, but don't worry; the strong, valiant, courage-

ous yeomen of Alberta are on the land now patiently putting in their crops. Through you, sir, may I tonight address a prayer from the bottom of my heart to Providence to bless their labour and give them a bumper crop.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene), I realize that there is a place in Canada almost as beautiful as my own riding of Peterborough. The hon. member spoke about the wonderful fish in Athabaska. I know he has never been to my riding and caught some of our wonderful muskellunge, because I believe Peterborough is the best game fishing district in the whole of Canada.
In talcing part in this debate, I consider it proper to offer some constructive suggestions and also do a little critieizing of the government, because I believe they deserve quite a bit of criticism. I happened to be in New York city, attending the assembly of the united nations, when the budget was brought down, and I noted that the New York newspapers placed a rather rosy appearance on it. But that rosy appearance was only on the surface, and was likely created only by the rose-coloured spectacles of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). When the average Canadian citizen had a chance to sit down with a copy of the budget speech before him and, with the aid of his own reading glasses, had an opportunity to digest the speech, he found it was not as rosy as it appeared at first glance. Indeed, one worker in my constituency said to me last Saturday that he thought the Minister of Finance was trying to follow m the footsteps of Barnurn, that great founder of the circus, and the man who coined the expression, "There's a sucker born every minute". He built his circus on that assumption.
However, today the people of Canada are not fooled as easily as they were in those days. Although we find some reductions in the income tax, the reductions which the people of Canada expected, after two years of peace, are not there. In fact, at the present time war taxes are still found in the budget. The Minister of Finance failed to remove luxury taxes on articles which are not luxuries at the present time. In that connection I would refer, first of all, to table silverware- knives, forks and spoons-which we require in our ordinary everyday lives. Veterans returning from the war had to pay a twenty-five per cent tax on all the flatware they required for their tables.
Another luxury tax is the one on alarm clocks. I am particularly interested in this.

The Budget-Mr. Fraser
because they are manufactured in my own city, and I do not think an alarm clock is a luxury.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It's a nuisance.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
A worker has to pay about S3 for an alarm clock, and on top of that a luxury tax of seventy-five cents. He must pay for the luxury of having an alarm clock to waken him in the morning so that he may go to work to earn a living, and to earn enough so that at the end of the week he may have the luxury of seeing taxes deducted from his wage cheque, by way of income tax.
As I said before, on the surface the budget looks all right, and it would seem that the government had been able to manage the country efficiently. But that is only on the surface; because the methods used by the government, as pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), to balance the budget, were certainly unethical, and methods which would not be allowed in any ordinary business in Canada or in any other country of the world. They have robbed Peter to pay Paul; they have taken money out of one pocket and put it into another. They have taken capital and used it for income. And when I say that I mean that their surplus is nothing more than the proceeds from the sale of war assets, war assets which were bought by the taxpayers of Canada during the years of war, and with their money. But today, instead of those proceeds being placed back in capital account to pay off part of our tremendous debt, they are shoved into income. We see listed the sum of 8372 million from the sale of war assets; and in this amount is included amounts received from the sale of ships which were built after the close of the war at a cost of S80.000, but which were sold off the ways for only S20.000. Then, office equipment was sold in the original crates at practically scrap prices. Many more millions of dollars could have been added to that $372 million from the safe of war assets if War Assets Corporation had been run on a businesslike basis, instead of on the catch^as-catch-can basis on which it was operated. According to a return tabled in my name on March 15, War Assets Corporation spent $210,631.08 last year, just to remodel and alter their office building in Montreal to take care of some of their 7.000 employees.
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance said there would be a reduction of twenty-nine per cent right across the board. This, too, was featured in the newspapers. But he did not tell us that that was only twenty-nine per cent off present income tax. and that even
with that percentage taken off it was far from putting the taxpayer back on the level of prewar years.
In 1938 a married man with his wife and two children, and with an income of $3,000, paid only $9 in taxes. But in 1948 the same man must pay $230 in taxes, or an amount twenty-five times as great as that he paid in 1938. A single man with an income of $3,000 paid $104 as a tax in 1938. while in 1948 the same man must pay $420. or four times the former amount.
No consideration whatsoever has been given to the fact that a married man with a family must look after and rear his children. Believe me, the man with a family finds today that it costs at least three times as much to bring them up as it did in 1938. on account of increased taxes and prices.
After a comparison of the taxes of 1918 with those of 1938, it is clear that there is absolutely no reason in the world why the government should not have a real instead of a false surplus this year, because they are getting in so much extra taxation, as compared with the amount taken in before the war. But they have not been able to declare that, real surplus because they have been extravagant in practically every department. Until they cut out that extravagance and waste they will never have a real surplus.
After paying income tax, the average family today finds that there is no chance of putting anything aside for a rainy day, no chance of saving anything to buy a home-even if they could buy one, because the government has certainly failed to provide homes for the people of Canada. The average family today finds it almost impossible, after paying income tax, to put aside a little money even to take a summer holiday. Prices are at an extremely high level. When I was speaking on the budget last year I said that the cost of living index was based, not on what you could buy but on what you could not buy. This year the cost of living index is still not right. If any hon. member doubts my word all he has to do is to go on the street and ask any housewife. She will soon tell him what is what. Here is a clipping with regard to that which states:
Finally admit cost of living index wrong The dominion bureau of statistics confirmed with figures Friday what any housewife could have told it a long time ago:	That the cost of
keeping the larder filled, the body clothed and the house furnished is considerably more than the official cost of living index.
Between August, 1939. and the end of 1946 the official increase was 26-1 per cent. By last month it had risen an additional 2-8 per cent.
But while these figures represented the official average advance, they did not give much indica-
The Budget-Mr. Fraser

tion of some of the things housewives have been howling about. Egg prices are 70 per cent higher than they averaged in the period 1935-39. In the same class are cheese, round steak, rolled rib roast, stewing beef, veal, bacon, lard, rice, beans, corn syrup and lemons.
The bureau computes its index by averaging the weighted representative price figure for each of six main essential item groups:	Fuel,
rent, foods, clothing, home furnishings and services and miscellaneous.
The food group advanced 47-4 per cent, clothing 31 -1 and home furnishings and services 28-2. Fuel moved ahead 10-3 per cent, rent (computed before the recent increase in domestic rentals), 9-2 and miscellaneous, 12-6.
The clipping does not say that at the present time, in order to secure things for her home, the housewife must wear out shoe leather going from store to store trying to find the things she wants. She can find1 no shirts for her husband, no diapers for the baby and no soap with which to wash them. Butter is up ten cents a pound; bacon is up over seventy per cent and is as scarce as hens' teeth. Rentals are supposed1 to be up only nine per cent, but try to find a house, an apartment, a room or even a dugout. You will find it is almost impossible. If you can get an unfurnished room, you will find that it will cost you almost as much as a furnished room cost in 1938, perhaps with board thrown in. The poor taxpayer has been getting it in the neck right along and it is time that more consideration was shown for him, especially the man in the low-income group.
It costs more for clothes, more for home supplies, and more for a car if you can get one. Then, added to that, in order to make the taxpayer's life more miserable, the government has retained the sales tax on electrical power. There is also the tax on telephones, and the transportation tax which gets you coming and going. A few departments have reduced their expenditures this year but they should have been cut far more. It would have been easy for them to cut expenditures this year, because some of the departments last year had carryovers from the war which they have not this year. Perhaps it is time that all departments had a real good house-cleaning. I feel quite sure that if a survey were made of each department hundreds of thousands of dollars could be lopped off the estimates.
I should like to give a few cases. While these may represent only small amounts, when enough small amounts are added up it runs into the millions. The government have been thinking in billions and I know it is hard for them to get down again to millions. They should remember that Canada has a population of only 12,000,000; we are not in the billion dollar class.

I had an answer a short time ago to a question I had asked regarding a piece of property the health department was renting on Parkdale avenue, Ottawa. The department is paying 818,000 a year rental for this property. There is no reason why that department should rent this building at the present time, because the government has buildings which were erected during the war and which would be suitable to house this department for the time being until building materials are more plentiful and until such time as building is needed in order to give employment to our people.
I said the rental of this building was $18,000 a year and I should like to figure this out in income taxes. A married man, with a wife and two children dependent upon him, paid no income tax on a $2,000 salary in 1938, but in 1948 his tax will be $36. On that basis it would take 500 taxpayers paying $36 each into the government treasury to look after this one rental. On top of that the health department is going to remodel the building. I have not the figures, but from what the return says I should judge that will run into another $18,000. That means another 500 taxpayers to look after the repairs, or a total of 1,000 taxpayers to look after the total expenses of one building which is not needed at all. That is certainly poor business on the part of the government. The return states that it is the intention of the Department of Public Works to have this building fitted up with special plumbing, sinks, partitions, et cetera, to meet the requirements of the health department.
I have another case, small as it may be, but, as I said before these small amounts run into the millions when they are added up. The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation issue a booklet every two months, or six times a year. This booklet is fifty-two pages in size and weighs about half a pound. I have one of them here. It does not help building in Canada one bit, because it deals only with housing in the United Kingdom, the United States, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Sweden and so on. It may be interesting but it does not help the veteran in Canada to get a home. I consider this is something that is absolutely useless and could be done away with.
Another thing that could be done away with because it is not of much use to Canada is the short-wave broadcasting station on the Atlantic coast. It is no use for Canada to try to keep up with the Joneses. This is costing us over $3,000 a day. I have here a clipping stating that the appropriations committee of the house of representatives in the

The Budget-Mr. Fraser
United States have definitely decided to do away with their short-wave station. This report, which is dated April 23, states:
House group kills programme of U.S. broadcasts abroad.
The state department's entire programme for broadcasting the American way of life to the world has been doomed by an appropriation sub-committee of the house of representatives, it was learned today.
Mr. Speaker, I imagine that you and most hon. members have visited a circus at one time and perhaps you carried water for the elephants, as I have done. You know what an elephant eats; you know how much they eat. At the present time the dominion government has a white elephant on its hands. This is just as much an elephant as any you have ever seen or ever expect to see. This year that white elephant is asking for $819,409 more than last year. In fact it is keeping the poor old taxpayer doubled up trying to pay for the feed of that elephant. The elephant I am speaking of is the film board. The film board perhaps is doing some good in putting out films for schools and for educational purposes, but the process of making these films is an extremely costly proposition. There are other ways in which the films could be made that would cost the county a great deal less money.
That same film board is at the present time subscribing to 127 magazines, periodicals and journals. I do not know what they cost, but I have my doubts whether there are ten men or women in the film board who ever read a quarter of these publications. This year nearly every branch of the film board is asking for more money. There does not seem to be any real check on the expenses of this outfit. I have a sample of their expense accounts here on my desk. Here is one for the period just before and during the 1945 election. It is for different members of the film board: trip to Quebec city, April 14, $200; May 28. another trip, $120; trip to Quebec, $300; May. another one, $350; other trips, $50 and $48. These are all for different persons and are dated around April, May and June. Here are two more trips, one for $150 and another for $300; June 7, trips to the maritimes, trips to Toronto. There are trips all over the country.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: One to Halifax?

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They will likely be going to Halifax for the election there.
We also have the Canadian information service, now under the Department of External Affairs. The cost this year of that information service as far as I can gather from the estimates is $241,200. That is not bad if it 83166-181
were not for the fact that nearly every department of the government advertised last year through the civil service commission for additional staff to handle advertising publicity in the respective departments. This extra help they are taking on in each department will amount to over $91,000, plus several other thousand dollars on which I have not been able to get the exact figures.
The Canadian information service, according to a return that was tabled in my name this year, show that in their offices in London they have three men receiving salaries, living allowance and travelling expenses; in Paris they have three men or women all receiving salaries, living allowance and expenses; in Washington they have twelve in the office, all receiving fairly good salaries, living allowance and travelling expenses; in New York they have seven, all receiving salaries and a living allowance which runs as high as $1,680, and travelling expenses-$424 is the highest. In all, the total is $82,872. They are getting nearly as bad as the C.C.F. in Saskatchewan, where they have jumped the expenditures on their information service from some $31,000 up to $73,000 in the last couple of years. They are using it to put out C.C.F. literature, or at all events they were. The Canadian information service, as I have said, have offices all over the country. If they are going to do a job they should keep it in one office and not have it in every branch of the government.
This year the following departments of the government have all increased their expenditures: Transport, up over $5,000,000; Secretary of State; Reconstruction and Supply, up over $10,000,000; Public Works, Public Archives, Prime Minister's Office. Post Office, National Revenue, up over $5,000,000; National Health and Welfare, up over $13,000,000; Mines and Resources, Legislation, Labour, Justice, Fisheries, External Affairs, up $1,779,000; Agriculture. I could go on for hours

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I know you do not like to hear of the government wasting the taxpayers' money.
I have a few suggestions to make before I sit down, and I hope that they are constructive. During the past year, many people have spoken to me about deductions from their income tax for medical expenses. The majority of people feel that the present exemption is not right. They consider that all medical and hospital expenses should be allowed, especially for those in the low-income brackets. A man with a salary or wage of $2,000 a year would have

The Budget-Mr. Fraser

to have medical and hospital expenses in excess of $80 a year before he could make any deduction for medical expenses.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Try the C.C.F. plan

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And you pay for it through the nose in Saskatchewan. If a man's medical and hospital expenses amount to $82 he could deduct $2 from his taxable income, and that is all. This question of deductions for medical expenses should have been considered by the Minister of Finance when making, up his budget. If he would allow all deductions for medical and hospital expenses we would have a healthier Canada, because people would feel a little more free to go to the doctor if they felt that there would be some relief for them. But at the present time there is absolutely none.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is always a problem, going to the doctor for relief.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If more people would go to the doctor before they are sick we would have much less sickness in Canada. An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.
Another method by which the taxpayer could be saved1 a few dollars is in the cashing of war savings certificates, some of which become due this year. The chartered banks of Canada should be allowed to cash these certificates for their customers whom they know and who have accounts with them. In that way the government would be protected; the holder of the certificate would be protected, and the bank would be protected'. As it is now holders of these certificates must take them to the post office and must wait for perhaps months for their money to come back to them, and there is the chance that their certificates might get lost as many certificates were lost when people were subscribing for them.
I should like to ask the minister a question. He is not in the house at the present time. Before he left the chamber he told me that he had a bad cold, and he excused himself. At that time I suggested to him that he go to his hotel and go to bed, That is the only way to get rid of a cold. His parliamentary assistant is in the house, and I shall put to him the question that I intended to put to the minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. member has any good suggestions they will reach the minister.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not a suggestion; it is a question. Is there anything in the income tax act which says that the taxpayer must

make out his own income tax return? If he is wrong he is penalized for it. If he makes a mistake they charge him extra. I know we are all told we have to make out our own income tax returns.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You make your own returns.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes. It is the job of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) to collect the revenue, but the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is, I understand, the one who checks the returns.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all; he has nothing to do with it.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It all has to go through the hands of the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the return is wrong the taxpayer is charged an extra tax. A simple form should be prepared by the Minister of National Revenue. On that form the taxpayer should be asked what is his income, what is his status, and what are his deductions. That form should be sent in to the minister's office and the minister's department should figure out what the tax is.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No. The law is that every man must assess himself.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know, but look at the mistakes which have been made. That is the reason I am bringing this up. I have a return here which proves I am right. It is dated February 14, 1947. The first question was:
How many income taxpayers (a) individual; (b) corporation were paid rebates during 1946?
The answer was:
(a)	1,312,112.
(b)	1,033.
That meant all kinds of extra work for the minister's department. It would have been much easier-

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There was tax deduction at the source.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes; that could be done too. The minister's department will eventually have to make out the taxes for the people. Last year there were $49,538,800 rebated to the individual taxpayer.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That shows good work.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It might be good work, but a lot of that rebate went away back to 1940 because the minister's department is so far behind in its work.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, it is not.

The Budget-Air. Winters

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps not now; the
department is gradually catching up. I know some people have not received final receipts for their 1943 returns yet.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Excuse me for interrupting. I can say that with reference to the assessments, if you take the district of Ottawa, at the end of December, 1946, 99-5 per cent of the 1945 returns which were made on April 30, 1946. were assessed and completed. You can-lot beat that record. I will admit that in some divisions, in some district offices it was away below that. We have had an enormous shortage of staff.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That proves what I have said. In Ottawa where they have the head office to look after their returns and do not have to bother with four or five different offices to check on them the return is looked at, checked, and sent out again, but with the district offices it is an entirely different proposition. In these offices they tell you that your return is all right. You make out your cheque and give it to them. Some months, or perhaps two or three years after, you are told that you owe an extra $2, $3, $4, $5, or perhaps S200, $300, $400 or S500, and then you are charged interest on that.
In closing, I wish to quote two paragraphs from an editorial of the Peterborough Examiner of May 1, which I believe hits the nail on the head.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which nail? I thought there were none left.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not mean wire nails.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Fingernails.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is only a figure of speech. The Secretary of State said "finger-nails." But the builders of Canada find1 it impossible to get nails of any kind.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Stick to income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How can you hit them on the head?

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Minister of National Health and Welfare suggests that I should stick to income tax. He does not know nails. Perhaps there are none left in his riding.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the editorial?

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The editorial reads as
follows:
Each citizen would be wise to balance some of his increases in living costs against the reduction in his income tax. Butter has just risen ten cents a pound; what does that mean to you in a year? What will the increase in your fuel bill be? Do these, and other increases leave you much of what you are supposed to gain by your tax reduction?
You will find that you are in the hole and very much so. I continue with the editorial:
It may be that the budget has hidden virtues which have escaped us. We hope so. But we shall not feel any benefits which may be inherent in it for some time. Meanwhile, it appears to us to do little except make certain adjustments designed to preserve the existing balance.
Mr. R . H. WINTERS (Queens-Lunenburg): Any hon. members 'who reflect the feeling of the house when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) brought down the budget on April 29 and any of those who represent the true feelings of their constituents, must, I am convinced, come to the conclusion that the budget was generally satisfactory to all Canadians and outstandingly satisfactory to the vast majority of them.
At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I wish to pay tribute to the former Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) who, in recent years, through his untiring efforts helped to develop Canada to the point where such a budget was possible. But for him it might well be that the relief granted would not have been anything like the amount it was. In saying this, I do not wish in any way to detract from the present Minister of Finance, who certainly started out on the right foot in presenting his first budget.
What was needed to counter the widespread criticism as well as to stimulate necessary production was a sizeable decrease in personal income tax. The relief afforded was beyond the hope of most. In a country the size of Canada it is entirely impossible to satisfy everybody. There will be complaints from private citizens and from opposition members. Many of these complaints may be bitter and a few of them may even be justified, but it cannot be denied that the government is steering a safe and steady course. It is the even breeze and not the squall that results in a ship's best over-all progress.
From Nova Scotia's point of view one of the main considerations in the dominion-provincial financial discussions is the matter of the small tax fields, particularly the electricity, amusement, and pari-mutuel taxes. The revenues from these sources in Nova Scotia are not large, but there is a worth-while principle involved if it is acknowledged that the provinces, in order to obtain a full measure of autonomy, are to have tax fields of their own. These particular fields can be regarded as emergency fields. They were entered into only during the war, when it was necessary to tap sources of revenue previously untouched. I share the opinion of the Hon. Angus L. Macdonald and the Nova Scotia government that the federal government should withdraw
2S36
The Budget-Mr. Winters

from these fields at the earliest possible date, and, having done so, should not return to them unless there is another emergency.
The budget speech dealt briefly with subsidies. This is a word that, in itself, is the antithesis of free enterprise because, ;f an industry or function can flourish on its own merits, subsidies are not necessary. It is only when industries are not self-supporting but when they are nevertheless essential to the over-all economic structure that subsidies a? we know them become necessary. Nova Scotia is in the unfortunate position of being concerned with subsidies probably more than any other province, and I know that in Canada there is an impression, either conscious or subconscious, that the particular subsidies which Nova Scotia is paid, or has been paid, for the operation of her coal mines, and is being paid on freight rates and other phases of her economy, are a shameful indication of the province's weakness. This impression does not reflect the true situation.
When one analyses the circumstances more closely, it becomes evident that this matter of subsidies is anything but one-sided. That Nova Scotia and other outlying provinces have subsidized Ontario and Quebec since confederation is well known and evidenced by many facts, among them being that the large percentage of our manufactured goods is obtained from these two provinces, and that in many instances the large taxable revenues in these provinces are derived from estates and other sources built on moneys funneling to them from the outlying provinces.
The transactions of the Canadian export board and the Canadian Commercial Corporation alone will serve to underline my point in this connection. In a reply tabled on March 17, 1947, to a question I placed on the order paper, it was shown that the total value of contracts awarded by the Canadian export board and the Canadian Commercial Corporation as of that date was $330,872,575. This amount was broken down by provinces as follows:
British Columbia	 $32,356,280
Alberta	 1,273,956
Saskatchewan	 70,990
Manitoba	 931,626
Ontario	 122,637,489
Quebec	 171,102,255
New Brunswick	 348.628
Nova Scotia	 2,151,351
A closer analysis will reveal that of this amount, by provinces, Ontario received $30 per capita, Quebec $47 per capita, and Nova Scotia $3-4 per capita. The over-all average for all of Canada was $27 per capita. On a percentage basis Ontario received 37 per cent, Quebec 51-5 per cent, and Nova Scotia -65

per cent. It might sting New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island members to know that their provinces received -105 per cent and zero per cent respectively.
It is true the above returns show that the prairie provinces fared rather badly, but when one considers the amounts accruing to these provinces from contracts for wheat, beef, hogs and other farm products, Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and Prairie Farm Assistance Act, it becomes clearly evident that the maritime provinces get anything but the best of the deal. British Columhm members will be pleased to know that their province stands third highest in point of benefits from the contracts in question.
I do not wish to create the impression that I am criticizing the manner in which the Canadian Commercial Corporation or its predecessor, the Canadian export board, have placed these contracts. I have seen no evidence of partiality and with very few exceptions I believe the contracts to have been awarded in the best possible way. I have the highest regard for Mr. Low and the other officers of the corporation. I am merely trying to show the disadvantages Nova Scotia suffers through force of circumstances and the fact that she is not a producer of products which are normally in primary demand by foreign countries.
When the question of loans to foreign countries was before the house, maritime members supported it strongly. We took the stand that being favourably located on the Atlantic seaboard, and with good harbour facilities available at Halifax. Saint John, Sydney, Lunenburg, Liverpool and elsewhere, we were naturally in line for a large return, because we have always felt that, based on tradition as well as practical considerations, our natural field was export to European and South American countries, the United States and other countries which are more readily accessible from our ports than from any other ports in Canada.
With such disappointing returns developing in the face of our optimistic expectations, the various members may draw their own conclusions as to how they would feel if the province they represent found itself in the same predicament.
At the risk of drawing this argument too fine, but with the purpose in mind of placing clearly before the house Nova Scotia's attitude toward the over-all economic set-up and this matter of subsidies, I should like to go a few steps farther, using as my basis this total amount of $330,872,575 in contracts awarded by the Canadian Commercial Corporation.
Quebec and Ontario together, with sixty-three per cent of the population in Canada, derived, from contracts let in these provinces,

The Budget-Mr. Winters
a financial return of 88-5 per cent of the total, whereas Nova Scotia, with five per cent of the population, received only -65 or slightly more than one-half of one per cent of the financial return. If one considers that the average return per capita for all of Canada from contracts let was $27, and that for Nova Scotia it was only $3-4, it is a simple matter to show that on this deal alone Nova Scotia subsidized the rest of Canada in the amount of approximately $15 million and, Mr. Speaker, this is by no means an isolated illustration. It goes on all the time, year in and year out. Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island are, in fact, subsidizing the rest of Canada, despite the fact that some of the other provinces choose to give the impression that they are subsidizing us. This is the reason why, when coal subsidies were removed some time ago, I stated in this house, during the debate on emergency powers, that Nova Scotians need not feel badly in accepting payment of subsidies, and that this practice is not nearly as iniquitous as many people would have us believe.
Then, too, we must not lose sight of the fact that many products are manufactured in central Canada under the protection of tariffs, and we in the outlying provinces are forced to buy from these sources goods that we could obtain cheaper from other countries if there were no tariffs. This, in our opinion, is a direct subsidy, paid by provinces such as Nova Scotia to central Canadian industry. This is an old and well recognized story, but I again wish to make it clear that these problems are real. Nova Scotians are realistic; they want to see Canada go forward as a nation, and if these tariffs help toward our industrial development as a country, we cannot oppose them; but Nova Scotia wants an equal opportunity to advance with the rest of Canada. I wish to emphasize again that we do not seek or wish any of our undertakings to be subsidized to the point where industry or labour feel they do not need to exert their greatest and most efficient efforts to achieve maximum output, but where subsidies are indicated in order to allow outlying provinces, having economic problems such as those facing the maritime provinces, to assume their rightful place in Canada's economy, we do not make any excuse for justifying them.
This inequality in Canada's economy is one of the reasons, too, why Nova Scotia was justified in seeking the best possible settlement under the dominion-provincial tax agreements, because the proposals offer a means of tapping the revenue of the more fortunate provinces and distributing it to the less fortunate provinces.

speechtext:
While dealing with Nova Scotia's economy, I should like to draw the attention of this house to a few problems respecting our fisheries. I will not deal with fishing operations at any great length at this time, because there will be another opportunity later, when the fisheries estimates are before the house; but I wish to say a few words about labour problems as they apply to our fishermen. Before doing so, however, I should like to express the view held by all fishermen that this budget is eminently satisfactory to them, in that it provides a good measure of relief from personal income tax. The policy of averaging incomes over three years is also meeting with universal approval. In Nova Scotia generally, and in Queens-Lunenburg in particular, we have always prided ourselves on the harmony existing between labour and management. Communities and towns are comparatively small, with the result that people in all walks of life grow up together as neighbours. Almost without exception they have known each other well, and I am aware of no other place Where there is less of what is commonly called "class distinction." Without fear of contradiction I can say that we have had happy community lives. During the war, returns from fishing were good, and when compared with many other industries it must be accepted that a relatively high standard of living obtained. Then suddenly into this harmonious picture were injected seeds of dissension, culminating in what may yet prove to be a ruinous strike in which the issue boiled down to one of union recognition, the union involved being the Canadian fishermen's union.
Let me say at this point that the lot of the fisherman has not always been happy. He was the poor relative in our working class. His hours were long and his returns small, but in
recent years the government has assumed its
283S
The Budget-Mr. Winters

rightful responsibility on his behalf, with the result that his status has been considerably improved. With respect to the recent strike, then, one cannot help seeking in one's mind the underlying reasons for the strange and contradictory developments. It came as a sad realization to us within the constituency, and a surprise to the rest of Canada, to know that the worm boring from within, as is so often said, was communism. We are usually led to believe and we generally accept as a fact that communism breeds on dissension and poverty, but in this instance neither of these elements was present. This was not a classical field for communism, and that fact, in itself, makes the happenings all the more sinister. That this element could come into communities where happy, harmonious relationships prevailed, and where pride in standard of living abounded, should be a matter of the gravest concern for every thinking Canadian.
That the fishermen should be entitled to collective bargaining and other union privileges is denied by no one; in fact I personally and, almost without exception, the fish operators feel that labour should be encouraged and guided in this direction for its own good and the good of the country at large. I am sure that if the fishermen wish to organize within the framework of applicable legislation they will be given every support and encouragement, so that they may have an opportunity of enjoying the benefits of collective bargaining. In fact the Nova Scotia government is enacting measures to provide the legal facilities.
As a class, fishermen must not be discriminated against, and I am sure they will find there is no such intention. The rank and file of the fishermen realize that the right to organize and enjo3T the benefits of unionization involves responsibility, and that they must develop their organization on a sound basis in order to inspire trust and confidence. It goes without saying that part of this responsibility is the selection of good leaders. No one denies the fishermen the right to choose their own leaders, but they will realize that in large measure the success they achieve as a union will depend upon the men they elect to direct them; and I am sure they are aware that their future is not associated with communism, which has shown itself to be vicious and irresponsible. The welfare of the fishermen is emphatically not its first consideration. As Hon. Angus L. Macdonald, premier of Nova Scotia, said when speaking in the Nova Scotia legislature, "communism is not a political party; it is a revolution".

Too often the farmer is the forgotten man in Nova Scotia's economy. Our farmers feel that in many respects the farm policy is based upon the western farm colony and overlooks the small farmer who is contributing in a worth-while way without any opportunity for a sizeable return. There are in Queens and Lunenburg counties hundreds of farmers struggling under what would be considered by western farmers to be extremely adverse conditions. It is almost impossible to obtain farm labour, and when it is available it is at rates which are almost prohibitive. Costs of feed are high, and the fear is that they will go higher. A recently authorized increase in the price to the western farmer of barley and oats resulted in an increase of feed prices in Nova Scotia which in many cases turned a self-supporting operation into a losing one. I refer particularly to poultry. At about the same time that the price of feeds was increased the ceiling on eggs was lifted as a measure of compensation, and at a later date it was completely removed. However, instead of the price of eggs going up it actually went down, and the farmers were forced to destroy thousands of chicks. It is hoped that the recent upward revision in the price of eggs sold under British contract will rectify this situation. I refer to the announcement made by the Minister of Agriculture in this house on April 30.
Another handicap to the farmers of Queens and Lunenburg counties is the lack of the bovine tuberculin test. This test has not been applied for some years, with the result that farmers in these two counties are not allowed to sell their stock in tuberculosis-free counties and are obliged to accept correspondingly lower prices for their products. I am well aware that there is an over-all shortage of qualified veterinarians in Canada, but I would impress upon the minister the great importance attached to this problem and urge him to take the necessary action to have these tests applied at the earliest possible day.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would say that Nova Scotia's economic problems are far-reaching. The budget as such did not provide a solution of our provincial problems, but we hope that the dominion-provincial financial agreements, which were presented last year and subsequently modified, will go a long way in that direction. The average individual in Nova Scotia feels that the budget has gone a long way to solve his own personal problems, and as such the citizens of the constituency of Queens-Lunenburg endorse it.

The Budget-Mr. McKay

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time I wish to discuss a subject which is of the utmost importance to western Canada; that is the subject of irrigation. This is now considered by the people of western Canada as of paramount importance to the rehabilitation of the dried-out areas of the western prairies. The interest in irrigation which has recently developed in western Canada is the logical result of the associating of memories of the drought-stricken prairies of the thirties with the evidence of the value of irrigation, which ha3 been so well demonstrated by successful projects in southern Alberta and in the semi-arid regions of the United States. One need hardly recall the suffering which the series of dry years brought to the prairie people, and in particular to the residents of southern Saskatchewan. The fear of those terrifying and depressing years still persists. That is the major reason why, during the past dozen or more years, people have been moving from southern Saskatchewan in such large numbers. A larger proportion of these people have abandoned farming entirely, since for them it was a hopeless venture. These farmers were so disillusioned that they decided to seek other means of making a livelihood. And because Saskatchewan is largely an agricultural province, people desirous of seeking other occupations were obliged in a great many cases to seek emploj'ment elsewhere.
The drift from Saskatchewan has been most alarming. The census of 1941 showed that the province had 25,000 people less than in 1931. When the natural increase of some 11,000 persons a year is added to this loss, it will be observed that in the decade 1931-41 more than 135,000 people have migrated from Saskatchewan, the great majority of them to British Columbia, eastern Canada or the United States. And I would point out that this vast loss occurred before the present C.C.F. government took office in that province; it took place during the regime of a Liberal administration. But no one would, I hope, be so unwise as to blame any provincial government for this trek from the Saskatchewan plains. It is the result of repeated years of drought; and no government has control over climatic conditions. If blame is to be placed anywhere for this situation, one must fix it on the federal governments of the nineties, and the first quarter of this century. While these governments could not control the weather in the area affected, they did have, at that time, control of immigration and colonization. It is now generally accepted in the west that the peopling of the Palliser
triangle was a grave mistake, and federal governments of the nineties, and even later, are responsible for this error. Certainly the people who settled there are not responsible, because they knew very little about the country when they settled in that particular region. Thousands of people from eastern Canada, the United States and Europe came to this area with faith in their hearts, and with the hope of making a good living on the land. They remained only to lose faith and to find poverty, where the promise of wealth was held out to them by colonization officials.
The rainfall in many parts of the region is too uncertain to permit of successful farming, except for those who can afford modern power machinery and large acreages of land. The early settlers had limited resources, and therefore in most cases were unable to cope with the vicissitudes of the drought-ridden areas. By dint of hard labour, and by depriving themselves and their families of the necessities of life, few have become independent; but they are all too few.
Why this mistake was made it is difficult to understand. Almost a hundred years ago Palliser reported that most of what is now populated country was little more than a semiarid desert. People were nevertheless induced to settle in that area, by the gift of free land by the federal authorities. Railways were constructed; towns and villages sprang into being, while the newcomers looked to the future with hope. Occasionally there was a good crop. Farmers then paid off their most pressing debts, allowing the remainder to wait in the hope of another bumper yield.
But there were more failures than big crops. In the past forty years, at least twenty crops were recorded as failures in a large part of southern Saskatchewan. That is the cause of the decline in population of that region in the west today. But despite this depopulation, there are still hundreds of thousands of people residing in the area of the Palliser triangle. In that area are many millions of dollars of investments in railways, elevators and other properties. The removal of this whole population to other regions is unthinkable, and quite unnecessary if the country were irrigated. And, despite unfavourable weather conditions at times, the people of southern Saskatchewan love the prairies. They are remaining in the hope that irrigation projects will make living there more pleasant and profitable in the future, and that Canada will soon realize that the irrigation of that area is practicable.
The region I have been discussing can produce great wealth in agricultural products. This has been amply shown when the rains
The Budget-Mr. McKay

come. The provision of irrigation works to provide moisture would meet the need when the rains fail. This huge area cannot be set aside as wasteland without seriously disturbing the national economy of the country. Many people and organizations are today advocating increased immigration to Canada. Thousands of newcomers to this nation could find homes within the Palliser triangle, if the region were irrigated.
It is necessary to provide water only during the crop growing season of a few weeks each year. Many small streams such as the Souris, Qu'Appelle, Long and Waseana creeks have sufficient spring flow, if conserved, to provide moisture for hundreds of thousands of acres of land, the finest in Canada.
The period of reconstruction following a devastating war has arrived. Irrigation of the Palliser triangle could make of the vast dried-out areas a populous and Eden-like garden of fertility. The value of irrigation has been well demonstrated in the Lethbridge district of Alberta and in scores of semi-arid regions of the central and northwest United States. These projects are rehabilitating farm land and have resulted in the production of millions of dollars worth of agricultural products.
More than 500,000 acres have been irrigated in Alberta and 4,500 successful farm units have been set up. Farms in the irrigated district now have assured yearly incomes. New industries have followed this development and employ many workers. To illustrate, I need only refer to the sugar refining industry which has contributed so largely to Alberta's economy. Last year this industry produced millions of pounds of sugar; in fact, eleven - per cent of Canada's 1946 consumption.
Irrigated farms also permit of more stock raising and dairying because a supply of fodder is assured. Ranges which supported one steer on forty acres now finish for market two animals per acre. Soil which formerly produced sixty-five cents worth of beef now produces $130 worth of sugar beets per acre. Land which could barely average ten bushels of wheat per acre now produces thirty bushels and upward. It is estimated that for every square mile irrigated the population in the district increased ten-fold.
That is only a small part of what irrigation can do for the prairie lands within the Palliser triangle. It will make the output of new wealth constant and will direct into the national economy a stream of revenue which will not fluctuate with recurring periods of drought. Irrigation has done great things in the United States. The following article

clipped from the Globe and Mail of April 30 of this year indicates what is happening in the United States:
The large scale "grass roots" movement like that now taking hold in the west is a proved device in the United States. Several years ago, to stimulate the development of irrigation in the northwestern states, a similar organization was set up. The results have been truly remarkable. Since the movement commenced, 5,000,000 dry acres have been placed "under ditch" and plans call for the extension of water facilities to a further 10,000,000. Washington has spent about one billion dollars on this work. If this figure seems extravagant, one need only balance it against dividends on investment. The total cash returns from crops in the reclaimed areas in the United States for the combined years of 1945 and 1946 equalled almost $900,000,000, or 90 per cent of capital outlay.
Subsidies and Prairie Farm Assistance Act benefits may temporarily relieve a condition and have served a useful purpose, but they cannot solve the problem of recurring drought. Irrigation is the only answer. The proposed irrigation scheme on the South Saskatchewan river would irrigate a large tract of land. The experience gained by the operation of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act justifies embarking on such a venture. The cost of such an enterprise on the Saskatchewan river would involve the expenditure of upwards of $25,000,000. This, together with other suggested projects, might even necessitate an expenditure of $100,000,000. But this programme would provide water for some 2,000,000 acres of excellent soil, and 20,000 farms of 100 acres each would be established. The servicing of the newly irrigated area would require thousands of people. In all, a project of this kind would support more than a quarter of a million population.
Such a development would create millions of dollars of new wealth. Small industries associated with agriculture would be set up. Sugar refining, canning, meat packing plants and dairying are accepted as certainties. Young people who seek employment elsewhere in Canada could find profitable employment in their own province. The drift of population from the prairies would be retarded, if not wholly stopped.
This new wealth will make a prosperous prairie region. As a result, eastern industries could not help but profit from the increased sales of consumer goods to the western provinces. But the major benefits are not to be measured in dollars and cents. The people in the west would have a new faith in confederation. They could look to the east with a feeling of friendship and appreciation. A new unity would result and a harmony prevail which hitherto has often been lacking.

The Budget

Mr. McMaster
The development of a full-scale irrigation programme for the prairies would be an investment in the future of Canada. I submit that such a project would be a sound reconstruction venture which would return tremendous dividends to the whole of Canada's economy. The undertaking would require a large initial outlay of capital, but the war proved to Canadians that what is physically possible is financially possible. Officials of P.F.R.A. state the project is physically possible, so I ask: Why the delay? The need is obvious. The land in the area is the world's finest and the water potential available in the Saskatchewan river and the other streams in the province. Canada cannot afford to procrastinate in this matter. The area must be rehabilitated. A western Canada irrigation programme should be the government's major reconstruction measure. I appeal to the government to embark on this national project without delay.

maintopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this late hour to make a few observations on the budget and with regard to several subjects dealt with therein. I should first like to say something about the method of bookkeeping which has been carried out during the last year by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). It is unfortunate perhaps that news was given out early in the year by the Minister of Finance that there would be a substantial surplus, because it started a great demand for lower taxes. The minister said frankly that perhaps this was not justified by the facts, and he stated, as reported on page 2553 of Hansard:
Economic conditions alone would hardly justify immediate tax reduction. As I have already stated, there are still substantial inflationary pressures pushing our prices and costs up. Reductions in taxes may add to these pressures in some measure, though they should reduce some of the demand for higher wage rates.
I would suggest that that is a poor foundation for a reduction in taxes unless a corresponding cut is made in the expenditures of the country. The matter is really worse than it looks. The minister has stated that the expected surplus of $352,000,000 was simply because we had received from War Assets $372,000,000 from the sale of certain articles, which by every system of good bookkeeping should have been capital return. If that had been capital return there would have been a deficit of $20,000,000.
I have watched with a great deal of concern the operations of the foreign exchange control board. I have felt certain over the past year, as I am today, that the operations of
the board will work a great hardship on the people of Canada, It will mean that we shall have to take an immense loss which we would have been saved if the exchange had been allowed to find its own level. It is a sort of system of subsidies which people do not appreciate and which benefits most perhaps those who need it least, and in the long run the loss to the country will be considerable. On page 17 of the 1946 report of the foreign exchange control board appears this statement:
Canada's external United States dollar assets were reduced by $330 million in 1946, of which $263 million is accounted for by the decline in liquid reserves of gold and United States dollars.
If I understand the operations of this board that means that we have lost $330 million just as surely as though we had spent it in another way and that we have nothing to show for it except perhaps greater trade with the United States. This must have been known to the board. It was so, because in the proceedings before the committee in the other place the governor of the bank said that would likely be the case and then he made the remarkable statement that he thought it would be good for Canada to import as much as she could, regardless of how it was to be paid for.
In the last year it has been stated that our trade with the United States was an adverse one of $603 million. That was progressively getting worse during the year. According to a recent statistical report for the month of March, that trend is continuing, because in that month our imports from the United States amounted to $136,606,000, while our exports to that country amounted to $79,453,000, showing an adverse balance of over $57,000,000, and if that is continued during the year it will mean a greater adverse balance than we had last year. It is likely to continue, because in the month of February our exports had dropped from approximately $79,000,000 to approximately $63,000,000. The latest report does not give the imports. But there was a falling off in our exports to the United States of $16,000,000 in February. If that continues, then as surely as anything in this world Canada will lose a substantial amount of money by the operations of the foreign exchange control board and this will be another debt to be shouldered by the people of Canada,
The minister expected a revenue of about $2,450 million during the present year and against that he had estimated ordinary expenditures of $1,285 million, or an increase over the previous year of about $52,000,000, and a very great increase over the year before that.

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
He has also other expenditures of $710 million, or total expenditures of $1,995 million. Yet nothing is said about the large amounts of money that must be advanced to the United Kingdom during the present year. About $600 million of the one and a quarter billion has already been given; another $600 million is to be advanced, and perhaps $300 million more will be advanced to other countries of the world on the three quarters of a billion dollar loan promised to them. So in the immediate future Canada will not be paying her way, because these are very doubtful assets, and the rate of interest paid by the people of Canada will increase to a great extent during the coming years.
There has been an advantage given to the taxpayers in Canada in all income brackets, but the advantages are much less for the taxpayer with a low income than the benefit he would nave received if some of the hidden taxes were removed. I have made a computation of some of these hidden taxes, using as a basis the amount that an ordinary man with a family would spend on these taxes. I have dealt with only four or five special taxes. I have dealt, of course, with the sales tax, which produces $328 million, or an average of $27 for every Canadian citizen. I have preferred to say that each ordinary citizen might spend $13.50 a year as his share of this sales tax, leaving the man in the higher income brackets, the wealthier people, to pay a considerably larger proportion. But the man in the lower brackets has to pay his share of the sugar tax, for instance, the soap tax and the amusement tax and for candy and other things like that which the children must have. I have found that the average man with a wife and two children would be paying $60 a year in these taxes.
On that basis I find that the ordinary family is paying a considerable amount of monej- in this hidden way, far more than the relief it is getting through the income tax deductions just made. I find that married men under the $3,000 bracket without children, who are saving in income tax, according to the latest statistics of taxpayers issued by the income tax office, $8,170,000, are paying $10,000,000 in these hidden taxes. That is, they have been saved $8,170,000 in income tax and they are paying 810,000,000 in hidden taxes. Married men, with an income less than $3,000, with a wife and one child, have a saving of $7,350,000, and they are paying hidden taxes amounting to $9,S50,000. Married men, with two children- and this is the favourite example given by the Minister of Finance-make a saving in the case

of those with incomes of under $3,000-I am dealing only with incomes of $3,000 or less

of $2,800,000. But actually the men in that class, including those who do not pay taxes at all, pay $13,500,000 in hidden taxes. Married men with three children save $1,300,000 and contribute to these hidden taxes about $7,000,000. Married men with four children save only $500,000 by these income tax reductions, yet contribute in hidden taxes, $9,000,000. The family with five children or more, because of the greater amount they must buy, save nothing but must pay in sales tax alone at least $15,000,000. I am speaking only of those with incomes of $3,000 or less.
Therefore 726,000 people of Canada have been saved $18 million. These same 726,000 people contribute the sum of $64 million to the treasury in these hidden taxes. These are all people in income brackets of less than $3,000. The minister has said that in these brackets he is relieving a great many taxpayers. The computation which I have made leads me to believe that, while it has relieved some, there are at least 720,000 single income taxpayers and about one million married taxpayers who are still paying taxes.
I have tried to prove my figures of who have paid sales taxes and other taxes by the number of families that receive family allowances. From the last report which I have at hand I find that 1.592,751 families receive family allowances. They have a total number of children of 3.638,030. On the basis of $60 for each family they would spend about $94 million in these taxes. There are 475,000 married people with no children who are spending on the basis of half the amount of $60 a family on these hidden taxes. They spend $14 million a year. If we take it in that way it would amount to $108 million that is spent by married men w'ith children and without children on these hidden taxes. For that reason I believe the minister should have reduced the sales taxes and these other hidden taxes. They are hidden taxes, but they affect the people more nearly and more severely than do the income taxes. They see the income tax; they know about it, bat these sales taxes they do not see. The larger the family, the more of these taxes they pay. For this reason I would say that the minister has not framed his budget in a way which will relieve the family man and the man in the lower income bracket. It will relieve them to only a small extent. It does give a measure of relief to some, but it does not go far enough to help those whom it should be his duty to help.
